speakerposition: topic
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Prime Minister) moved that the House go again into Committee of Supply.

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
['Well, I have not in my reading observed any statement which would give me that information, but I fancy it would take considerably over one billion of dollars. I understand that the American railway carriers claim from the United States Government something over $900,000,000 to put their roads back where they were prior to their being under federal control, and it is asserted that that would not commence to meet their legal and valid demands. I refer to the railway conditions in the United States only for the purpose of indicating that there is a railway problem in that country just as there is in this, and by way also of opposing the possible idea that our condition is entirely due to circumstances for which this country alone is responsible.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what are the principal considerations which suggest the appointment of a committee, and how might such a committee function to the advantage of Parliament and of the country? The facts which I have just presented to the House in relation to the financial condition of our railways surely indicate the existence of a situation that must be considered, studied and dealt with by this Parliament and by the country. It involves the imposition of heavy taxation, and no intelligent and reflecting man will deny that the situation demands the gravest thought and study on the part of every Canadian who is interested in the present and future of his country. I suggest further that a large deliberative body or assembly such as this House of

Commons is hardly suitable for the effective consideration of this problem. That is an assertion which cannot safely be contradicted; in fact, one might postulate that proposition. Our experience also shows that for the purpose of reaching constructive ideas and informing the members of the House and the people generally, as well as in reaching a definite public policy for the future, a small parliamentary committee affords the best means. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, on general principles a committee of Parliament should be appointed to consider the railway situation in itself as well as in its relation to all the other interests of the country.
I should like also to suggest for the consideration of the House that Parliament requires information upon this question. I am not reflecting upon the knowledge which any hon. gentleman has or upon his capacity to obtain it and to utilize it when he gets it. But I think I may safely say that members of this House and the people of the country generally, outside of those who are engaged in the railway business as a vocation, are sadly in need of information on this subject. It is only when we are armed with knowledge that we can embark upon any definite policy for the future or that we can safely legislate. I think that one might say, without reflecting on past Parliaments, that a great many of our railway difficulties to-day are due to the fact that Parliament itself was not informed. The governments of the day thought that they themselves were informed, and possibly they were; but if there had been on the part of Parliament that degree of accurate knowledge regarding the matter with which the government itself was dealing, the government policy might have indicated greater wisdom than it did.
Newspaper correspondents are beginning to say that our railway affairs had better be handed over to business men, and that members of Parliament and the Government would consent to this transfer of duties. I have all my life been looking for an accurate definition of this omnipotent so-called business man who is taken from his hiding place every time the nation is in great trouble. For my part, I do not admit the capacity of these business men to deal with the situation any better than anybody else, unless they are informed upon the subject-and I doubt very much that they are so informed at the present time. However, that is a point which I feel I need not elaborate; it is a self-evident proposition that before we take further steps in connection with the railway problem in this country, Parliament should be informed. I am not emphasizing the fact that the Government should be informed. That is their duty; we assume that they will take every possible step to inform themselves, but I go further and say that it is equally the duty of Parliament to be informed. I say with little trepidation that a parliamentary committee can do more to inform Parliament and the country upon this question than any other body which can be suggested. The presence of the management of the Canadian National Railway system before a committee of Parliament for a few days annually could not fail to inform Parliament and the country. There will be made public facts which cannot be made public to-day by reports through the Minister of Railways or the Government. Foolish and absurd statements are being made day after day, predicted upon assumptions which are not based upon facts. If there is anything dangerous to the country at the present time in relation to a great and important public service, it is having Parliament and the country debating the problem upon facts which have not been established. Expert opinion could be brought before that committee to advise members of the committee, in the hope that that advice, if worthy of credence and acceptance, could be extended through the committee to Parliament, and thus gradually get out into the country, so that sound and intelligent public opinion could be formed upon this issue. A committee before which the management might appear would also afford an opportunity to the management to give to the country their views of the situation, and generally speaking, a standing committee of this House is the best and, I am almost bold enough to say, the only method by which Parliament and the country can be educated as they should be upon this problem at the present time.
We must not forget that when a Government owns and operates a railway with a deficit of $50,000,000 in 1920 and a probable deficit of $100,000,000 in 1921, it is not likely to receive fair treatment from the people. The quality of the management will not be fairly judged by the country unless that management have an opportunity of putting before the people their side of the story of their management. Further, in years past in connection with the railway problem, when, perhaps, it was largely the function of railways to exploit the country, we passed laws to protect the public against the carriers. The situation', "

is very much changed. The railway question will never again appear before the public in the exact form in which it did from ten years bade to twenty-five or thirty years preceding that. The country to-day is the owner of a great system; the people are the shareholders; they must pay out of their pockets any operating deficits; they must provide capital for the continuance and operation of the road. While heretofore it was, perhaps, largely the work of Parliament and statutory bodies created by Parliament to protect the public against the carriers, it may be that now our true function will be to protect the carriers against the public. There is, at least, something in that statement.
At Six O'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at Eight o'clock."]

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to move an amendment which is substantially the same as the notice of motion which stood in my name for several days and which had relation to the appointment of a committee to be known as the Railway and Shipping Committee. Last evening, the House will remember, I moved for the discharge of that motion from the Order Paper. I did so because I was likely to be absent from the House during the next few days, and also because, even were I sure of being here continuously, there was considerable doubt as to when I might have an opportunity of moving that motion. I was anxious to be able to present it to the House as early as possible, and after consultation with the Prime Minister last evening, I made the motion for the discharge of that motion from the Order Paper, which was unanimously carried by the House. Upon giving notice this afternoon to the Prime Minister of the text of this amendment, he pointed out to me that his position would be somewhat prejudiced by my moving it on a motion to go into Supply, and that possibly he might not have consented last evening to my motion being discharged from the Order Paper had he understood that this amendment would be moved to-day on the motion to go into Supply. I refer to this fact merely to say that I do not desire to prejudice the position of my right hon. friend or his supporters, particularly if any embarrassment to them were due to any act or word of my own. Therefore, upon the conclusion of the debate on this amendment, I shall ask the House for leave to withdraw it. It will be understood, of course, that when the right hon. the Prime Minister comes to move for the appointment of a committee, which, I understand, he has intimated he will do, there will then be an opportunity for me or any other hon. gentleman to move for additions to the powers of that committee, if in my judgment or theirs it is felt that those powers are too limited.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I dislike interrupting the hon. gentleman, but did he say that the amendment which he is about to move this afternoon is substantially the same as the motion he got leave to withdraw yesterday? If so, in what respect do they differ?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
The only respect in which they differ is that the period of continuance of the suggested committee is limited, in this amendment, to this session, and it was my intention to incorporate that amendment in the original motion had I moved it. Now, the purpose of the amendment is disclosed in the text itself; the reading of it will show the intended functions of the committee if this House decides to establish it. The name of the committee also suggests substantially the range of its jurisdiction. I think that such a committee should have the right and power to enquire into substantial matters of policy connected with the management and administration of the Government owned and controlled railway system of this country, and as well the shipping, which is known as the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. I should hope that the work of this committee, if it were appointed, would be of a substantial and informative character; if it were not, it would fail to fulfil the terms which I have in mind at the moment. It is not my intention that there should be conferred

upon this committee supervisory or administrative powers over railway matters-and when I refer to railway matters, the House, I trust, will bear in mind that I have reference only to the system of railways known as the Canadian National Railways. I should hope that this committee would be the means of supplying a great deal of information to the public in connection with the government-owned system of roads; that it would be the instrument by which the management of this railway system could convey to the public, who are its owners, an account of their stewardship, and in this manner give a review of existing or contemplated policies of the Board. I should hope that this committee, if established, would establish between the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian public some such relationships as exist between an ordinary commercial enterprise and its shareholders. I should hope that there would be established, as between the management and Parliament, at least the relationship which ordinarily exists in commercial concerns between the management and the board of directors or the shareholders. Now, Mr. Speaker, I realize that asking for the creation of a committee with such wide powers is perhaps somewhat unusual in our parliamentary experience, and I therefore realize very clearly I trust that in order to induce Parliament to accept my proposal I must convince, or should endeavour to convince Parliament that a serious problem confronts us to-day. If I succeed in doing so I think it should follow that the proposal contained in the amendment should be granted, and that a committee, to whom should be granted unusual powers, should be set up to meet an unusual situation. In order to do this I must refer to certain matters relating to dhe Canadian National Railway system, and particularly to the economic condition of that system. I do so primarily for the purpose of impressing ithe House, if I can, with the gravity of the situation now confronting it.
'A few days ago the Minister of Railways presented to the House what is known as the annual railway statement, which statement contained a great deal of valuable and important information regarding the Canadian National Railway system. I do not know that the statement which the minister gave could have been more complete without it becoming somewhat burdensome to himself and to the house. However, we learned from the minister that there are in Canada to-day 17,000 miles 
of railway controlled by the Government, and possibly this mileage shall later be increased by the acquisition of the Grand Trunk Railway. We learned that in 1919 there was a deficit of $48,000,000 on account of operating and fixed charges, that in 1920 there was an operating deficit of $37,000,000, and that in 1920 there was a deficit of $70,000,000 on account of operations and fixed charges. We further learned that 95 per cent of the gross revenue of the system was consumed by two items alone- wages and fuel. We also learned from the statement that it cost $1.24 and a fraction to earn a dollar during the past year. The minister on that occasion likewise gave to the House his statement of net earnings for the current year, the railway year being the calendar year. He estimates a deficit of $50,000,000 on account of operating and fixed charges, and including interest on advances to the Canadian Northern Railway he calculates that this deficit will be increased to $60,000,000. This is reached by taking into consideration a possible decrease in wages, in the cost of materials, and by effecting economies which I fancy he hopes to be able to successfully introduce. So you see that the deficit in 1919 was very substantial, it was very substantial in 1920, and I suggest there is little or no evidence that if will be any less in 1921 notwithstanding the minister's estimate-in fact everything known to us suggests a very much greater deficit than we had in 1920.
Now considering the commercial and trading conditions of the world, the conditions of the European exchanges, the decrease in the productive powers of Canada and all other countries, the fact that even in Canada during the past three or four months the producers of lumber, fish, coal, iron and steel have reduced production [DOT]-I think it is probably a fair estimate to say that in the Prairie Provinces there will be a diminution in the production of wheat, largely owing to the fact that the cost of production is abnormally high, and the markets and prices are not very reassuring; -taking all these conditions into consideration I think it is fair to say that when the current railway year ends on December 31 this year we shall learn that a deficit considerably in excess of the deficit of 1920 confronts this country, and that I am sure will be regarded as a very serious situation. But the condition of a railway is not altogether revealed even by the operating results. It is true that the deficit of 1920 is, in itself, sufficiently staggering. It is also

I have no doubt, true and well known to hon. gentlemen that it is extremely desirable that a road should have more than a mere surplus of operating income; it is extremely desirable that it should build up a reserve. The Canadian National Railway system, in the face of the existing deficits, was unable to build up, or to add to, reserve. Further, the failure to have an operating income upon the credit side, the failure to be able to earn anything to add to a reserve, affects the credit of a railway company, and doubtless the borrowing capacity of the Canadian National Railway system has been disastrously affected by the result of the operations of last year. I think I am correct in saying that to-day the Canadian National Railway system would be unable to borrow any money in the markets of the world without the guarantee and backing of the Canadian Government. That being so, and I hardly think anybody can question my statement, I feel compelled to say, although very regretfully, that at the moment our National Railway system is practically bankrupt. In ordinary affairs an individual, or a commercial concern, is not considered bankrupt while they are able to pay and meet the demands of their creditors; but it is altogether different in connection with a railway system. As soon as a railway system reaches the condition that it is unable to borrow upon favourable terms it is bankrupt-because the operations of a railway never cease, it must be continually expanding. Further, we are all aware that during the past four or five years a great deal of money should have been spent upon maintenance, development and construction work, in connection with our railways. This has been deferred. I am not criticising anybody for so doing; I should say that that was good business policy. But nevertheless that fact must be taken into consideration in a review of railway conditions to-day. I make the statement, not authoritatively of course, but I think I am well within the mark, that no less a sum than $150,000,000 should this year be expended upon the Canadian National Railway system for maintenance, and improvements in order to prevent the impairment of our railway assets. That, Mr. Speaker, is a serious situation to contemplate, and I have not the slightest doubt that every hon. gentleman is impressed with its seriousness, particularly when coupled with the fact that we are facing for the current year such a large deficit.
Now, we can hardly hope to increase our railway revenues by a further increase in freight or passenger rates. It may be fairly stated, I think, that to-day our freight rates are at such a figure that they adversely affect the production of goods and our domestic and export trade. These high freight rates in turn contribute to the continued high price of commodities, thus lessening the ordinary exchange of goods and the total volume of the production of the country and their consumption, which in turn leads to unemployment. I have no doubt also that the fact that a great deal of maintenance work on our railways has been deferred also contributes to unemployment. And I think I may with greater confidence say that our passenger rates at least have reached that point when it would be inadvisable to further increase them. The statement of the Minister of Railways indicates a decline of 9.45 per cent in the number of passengers carried per mile in 1920 as compared with 1919. I think I am reflecting probably the judgment of the average member of this House when I say that our passenger rates might be reduced somewhat and thus stimulate the earning power of our railways. Therefore I say that we cannot well look to increasing railway revenues for the current calendar year by increasing freight or passenger rates; on the contrary not at all improbable that better financial results might be obtained by here and there a slight diminution in the rates.
Now, Sir, I do not refer to the financial condition of our railways with any degree of pleasure. It is not a condition that one would care to proclaim in Parliament in a malicious spirit or to injure his country; but facts must sometimes be faced boldly and courageously, and I think it is far better that Parliament and the country should realize the actual situation confronting us.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: And in other countries also.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
Yes, I am going to refer to that. There is some comfort in the reflection that in other countries approximating conditions prevail. When one thinks of the great extent of this Dominion, of the sparseness of its population, of the lack of development of our natural resources, and of the physical condition of a great deal of the country through which our railway system operates, it is not surprising to find the present results. I am sure we all have hope for the future. This country has the capacity to expand com-

mercially and otherwise, and it certainly shall, but of course in the immediate future our problem is a very serious one. I do not think that our position should be prejudiced by the fact that the other great railway system in this country presents a very much better showing for the past fiscalyear. I have never been able to appreciate why a statement of the financial condition of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company can be expected to contribute to the solution of our own railway problem. There are many obvious reasons why that system is in such a relatively flourishing condition to-day. The two systems are unlike and cannot be compared. To my mind it contributes very little to clearing the general situation to find so many flattering commendations made of the one road and so many unreasoned and unreasonable condemnations of the other.
Of course, a great deal of the present situation is due to the conditions ensuing from the war, and, as has been suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean, York) opposite, that fact has left similar results in many other countries. It would be very interesting just for the moment to look at the railway situation in the United States, where conditions are much the same as here, except that that country has a much greater population and is more fully developed. In 1920 it cost the American railways on an average $93.59 for every $100 earned; in 1919 the operating ratio was $85.25; in 1918, $81.54; in 1917, $66.46. The net operating income of the United States railways of the first class dropped from the high level of $934,000,000 in 1917 to $62,000,000 in 1920. In January, 1921, the operating deficit of 143 railways in the United States was $3,000,000, compared with a net operating income of $42,000,000 just a year before, in January, 1920. This, of course, indicates the existence of fundamental conditions prevailing in the United States as in this country which affect very greatly the railway situation. In March of last year the American railways passed from federal control back to their owners, the transfer being made under the provisions of the United States Transportation Act of 1920. The legislators of that country evidently felt that the future of their railway systems was not too fully assured, because in the Transportation Act they made provision for a stated income from earnings for these railways- a provision which had not previously existed. At present the United States railways are entitled to a minimum dividend of five per cent upon the value of the road and a minimum of, six

per cent. If an amount in excess of the six per cent is earned, the difference is divided between the railways and the nation as a reserve fund. The reserve fund belonging to the carriers is to be used by them for almost any railway purpose, while the proportion of the excess going to the United States Government is to be used by way of loans or advances to their railway systems. Further, the United States Transportation Act of last year provided for the voting of a revolving fund of $300,000,000, to be used for the purpose of aiding roads seeking financial support or assistance. That amount, I fancy, will meet but a small proportion of the applications for loans which will be made by the American roads.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member if he will be good enough to give an estimate of the amount that the roads of the United States will require to place them on a safe footing for the year?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
Well, I have not in my reading observed any statement which would give me that information, but I fancy it would take considerably over one billion of dollars. I understand that the American railway carriers claim from the United States Government something over $900,000,000 to put their roads back where they were prior to their being under federal control, and it is asserted that that would not commence to meet their legal and valid demands. I refer to the railway conditions in the United States only for the purpose of indicating that there is a railway problem in that country just as there is in this, and by way also of opposing the possible idea that our condition is entirely due to circumstances for which this country alone is responsible.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what are the principal considerations which suggest the appointment of a committee, and how might such a committee function to the advantage of Parliament and of the country? The facts which I have just presented to the House in relation to the financial condition of our railways surely indicate the existence of a situation that must be considered, studied and dealt with by this Parliament and by the country. It involves the imposition of heavy taxation, and no intelligent and reflecting man will deny that the situation demands the gravest thought and study on the part of every Canadian who is interested in the present and future of his country. I suggest further that a large deliberative body or assembly such as this House of

Commons is hardly suitable for the effective consideration of this problem. That is an assertion which cannot safely be contradicted; in fact, one might postulate that proposition. Our experience also shows that for the purpose of reaching constructive ideas and informing the members of the House and the people generally, as well as in reaching a definite public policy for the future, a small parliamentary committee affords the best means. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, on general principles a committee of Parliament should be appointed to consider the railway situation in itself as well as in its relation to all the other interests of the country.
I should like also to suggest for the consideration of the House that Parliament requires information upon this question. I am not reflecting upon the knowledge which any hon. gentleman has or upon his capacity to obtain it and to utilize it when he gets it. But I think I may safely say that members of this House and the people of the country generally, outside of those who are engaged in the railway business as a vocation, are sadly in need of information on this subject. It is only when we are armed with knowledge that we can embark upon any definite policy for the future or that we can safely legislate. I think that one might say, without reflecting on past Parliaments, that a great many of our railway difficulties to-day are due to the fact that Parliament itself was not informed. The governments of the day thought that they themselves were informed, and possibly they were; but if there had been on the part of Parliament that degree of accurate knowledge regarding the matter with which the government itself was dealing, the government policy might have indicated greater wisdom than it did.
Newspaper correspondents are beginning to say that our railway affairs had better be handed over to business men, and that members of Parliament and the Government would consent to this transfer of duties. I have all my life been looking for an accurate definition of this omnipotent so-called business man who is taken from his hiding place every time the nation is in great trouble. For my part, I do not admit the capacity of these business men to deal with the situation any better than anybody else, unless they are informed upon the subject-and I doubt very much that they are so informed at the present time. However, that is a point which I feel I need not elaborate; it is a self-evident proposition that before we take further steps in connection with the railway problem in this country, Parliament should be informed. I am not emphasizing the fact that the Government should be informed. That is their duty; we assume that they will take every possible step to inform themselves, but I go further and say that it is equally the duty of Parliament to be informed. I say with little trepidation that a parliamentary committee can do more to inform Parliament and the country upon this question than any other body which can be suggested. The presence of the management of the Canadian National Railway system before a committee of Parliament for a few days annually could not fail to inform Parliament and the country. There will be made public facts which cannot be made public to-day by reports through the Minister of Railways or the Government. Foolish and absurd statements are being made day after day, predicted upon assumptions which are not based upon facts. If there is anything dangerous to the country at the present time in relation to a great and important public service, it is having Parliament and the country debating the problem upon facts which have not been established. Expert opinion could be brought before that committee to advise members of the committee, in the hope that that advice, if worthy of credence and acceptance, could be extended through the committee to Parliament, and thus gradually get out into the country, so that sound and intelligent public opinion could be formed upon this issue. A committee before which the management might appear would also afford an opportunity to the management to give to the country their views of the situation, and generally speaking, a standing committee of this House is the best and, I am almost bold enough to say, the only method by which Parliament and the country can be educated as they should be upon this problem at the present time.
We must not forget that when a Government owns and operates a railway with a deficit of $50,000,000 in 1920 and a probable deficit of $100,000,000 in 1921, it is not likely to receive fair treatment from the people. The quality of the management will not be fairly judged by the country unless that management have an opportunity of putting before the people their side of the story of their management. Further, in years past in connection with the railway problem, when, perhaps, it was largely the function of railways to exploit the country, we passed laws to protect the public against the carriers. The situation



is very much changed. The railway question will never again appear before the public in the exact form in which it did from ten years bade to twenty-five or thirty years preceding that. The country to-day is the owner of a great system; the people are the shareholders; they must pay out of their pockets any operating deficits; they must provide capital for the continuance and operation of the road. While heretofore it was, perhaps, largely the work of Parliament and statutory bodies created by Parliament to protect the public against the carriers, it may be that now our true function will be to protect the carriers against the public. There is, at least, something in that statement.
At Six O'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
At six o'clock I was urging upon the House that in connection with the railway question it was desirable that Parliament and the country should be informed, and that by such means alone could we develop in this country a public opinion that would aid in the solution of the railway problem. I think it is a fact that there is to-day very little public opinion in this country upon the railway issue, largely because Parliament has failed in recent years to he informed itself, and through it the country. I was suggesting to the House that a committee to which would be granted very large and extensive powers, perhaps broader than those to which we have been accustomed in the past, would aid in the formation of constructive views in Canada, which would be found of some value in the early future. Now if we cannot

get information and develop constructive ideas, and assist the public in developing sound constructive ideas upon the railway question, as things go on at present, how is this information to be obtained and disseminated throughout the country in order that the conditions I have suggested might be brought about? The Minister of Railways cannot inform Parliament upon this question, so big has it become. He would need to be a superman, if there is such a person, to do so. It would be an impossible task to impose upon any minister to keep Parliament and the country fully informed upon so vast and intricate a problem. The Government cannot do it. It is their declared policy deliberately to abstain from intervening in the administration of the railway, and, so far as I know, the Government are living up to that policy, and I trust they will continue to do so. One thing is certain, and that is that government ownership and government control could not last twenty-four hours in this country if there was direct interference in the administration of the railways by the Government or by members of Parliament. Therefore, the declaration of Government policy precludes Parliament or the country from being informed by the Government. That eliminates the two probable sources from which the necessary information could be obtained.
Possibly a good way of strengthening one's position in such a case as I am endeavouring to make out would be to give a few illustrations of what I think a committee of the nature' I suggest might do. I may astound some hon. gentlemen -in the House and possibly some members of the Government, when I state some of the problems which I think might very properly and very profitably be committed to the committee for inquiry and investigation. Take the Hudson Bay railway. I do not know if other hon. gentlemen have had the experience I have had in connection with this public undertaking, but I think in all my experience I have yet failed to meet a Canadian citizen who thought this project would be a success. Yet the two historic political parties of this country have, I think, approved the project. I am not saying it is inherently weak and destined to absolute failure, just because that has been my experience, but as far as I am concerned, I should hesitate to commit the country to the completion of that undertaking until I had further information about it. It has not yet been settled that the Hudson Bay route is a feasible or practicable shipping route. In

fact, the Hudson Bay port selected, is not now deemed by the former friends of the project to have been properly selected. The very successful export of a cargo of wheat from Vancouver a few weeks ago has also given to the Hudson Bay undertaking an altogether different colouring. I quite agree that it is futile to deliberate upon past mistakes, but something might still be saved if it were the judgment of Parliament and the country that the project should not go to completion. How are we to be informed upon the subject? I know of no other way, or of no better way, at least, than by committing the consideration of that question to a Parliamentary committee. I do not believe there is any other method which would so promptly and effectually develop public opinion one way or the other upon that question. I think that is a matter which might very properly be committed to a Parliamentary committee, which I believe could do splendid work in considering it.
I will give another illustration in which the people of my province and of the Maritime Provinces generally are much interested. I refer to the operations of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. Parliament, of course, is cognizant of the fact that during the war the Canadian Government built a number of ships; it matters not what their number is, or their tonnage, or the motives which moved the Government to embark upon that policy. When the ships were constructed, it became necessary for the Government to adopt some method of operating them, and eventually they committed them to the Canadian National Railways for operation. That department did not seek the transfer of these ships; they were rather imposed upon them by the Government. I do not know that the Government is open to any criticism for so doing, but the Government have never formulated any definite and irrevocable policy as to the operation of these ships. Assigning them to the Canadian National Railways was only a temporary disposition of the matter. At the moment, I take it that the Government is free to vary their policy, established as I have indicated, and adopt a different policy, and if possible, a better policy. From maritime ports to-day, and also from American ports via our maritime ports, there are running four privately-owned steamship lines connecting with Newfoundland. These services have been built up in the course of years, after a great deal of trouble, risk, anxiety, and considerable investment of capital. All the require-
100J
ments of the Maritime Provinces and of the rest of Canada and of the ports of New York, Boston, and St. John's, Newfoundland, were fairly well satisfied with the shipping facilities provided by these four privately-owned services to which I have referred. Recently the Canadian Government Merchant Marine have placed in that service three or four boats. Those boats are losing a great deal of money in that service. There has been a curtailment of traffic. The privately-owned lines are also losing money.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
May I ask my
hon. friend how he knows that the Canadian Government ships are losing money on that route?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I know positively that nothing else is possible than the loss of money by the boats of the Canadian Merchant Marine that are now engaged in that Newfoundland service. I say to my hon. friend that nothing else would be possible, and I am so informed by men who know the shipping business just as well as those who are operating the Merchant Marine.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Or better.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
I therefore accept it as a positive fact that my statement is correct and incontrovertible. But even if my hon. friend were right and I wrong, I submit it as a fair proposition that the Canadian Merchant Marine have no right to interfere with established companies who, in the course of years, have developed a service which is satisfactory to the people generally. It is unfair and unjust, and you cannot get the people of this country very long to support such a policy. These privately owned companies pay their taxes, and they are at the present time losing money. The Canadian Merchant Marine are losing money, and they ask the owners of these companies to help pay the deficit encountered in their operations. As a matter of sound policy, this is wrong, and it is not fair treatment to the people who are engaged in that service to-day. And I do not believe that the people of the country will take any different position from the one I have just stated in this connection.
However, it would be very difficult, I take it, for me to persuade hon. gentlemen on either side to abandon the present policy unless I were able to demonstrate conclusively the facts upon which I base my conclusions. I do not think that any mem-

ber of Parliament has the right to occupy the time of his fellow members and ask them to reach a conclusion unless he knows his subject and is able to demonstrate the soundness of the conclusion which he hopes to impress upon them. I can quite understand, if I ventured upon such a course in this Parliament, I might be questioned as to my facts, and I am not sure that I could obtain them very easily without the information available through a committee. If a committee were appointed with jurisdiction over the matter of shipping, I should be entitled, I assume, to summon before that committee the managers of the company and the owners of privately-owned companies operating in the particular area to which I referred a moment ago, to have the opinion of everybody, and a general exchange of views; and in the end, that committee, if composed of capable men, would be able to reach a very safe and sane conclusion. If their finding were a sound one, I feel sure it would be accepted by Parliament and by the Government. But I want to say to the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne), that I am referring only to one particular service; I am not urging that the whole fleet of the Canadian Merchant Marine should be withdrawn from service. I am sure, however, that a great many of these steamships might profitably be sold, particularly the smaller ones operating from eastern ports. It is far better, if you wish to develop commerce and have a successful merchant marine in this country, to dispose of these ships at favourable prices and on satisfactory terms as to payment, to Canadians, if they will take the ships, because the history of the world is abundantly clear that all commerce is after all developed by the initiative of private individuals and not by governments or by ships.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: So are high rates for all kinds of transportation.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
There is no possibility of excessive freight charges today, with ten million tons of shipping more than before the war, two and a-half million tons of shipping being idle in the British ports to-day, and one thousand ships laid up in American ports. In these circumstances it is unlikely that the world will lack competition in the future. But, I repeat, the point I want to make is that it is extremely foolish and unprofitable for the Government to be operating boats at a loss on routes which are amply served by existing fleets owned by private individuals.

I do not propose detaining the House by citing matters which I think a committee might very well inquire into. If hon. gentlemen will permit me, I should like, in fancy, to see the heads of the railway management before this committee, if it is established. What is more natural than that the committee should have before them the general manager to go over the annual financial statement and thoroughly explain it, and to have matters which have not been submitted to Parliament placed before them? Would any public interest suffer, or would the railways be prejudiced by an exposure of all relevant and important facts? Would it not aid in the development of sound public opinion on such matters if this were done? There can be no difficulty in convincing one that great benefit would accrue from a discussion of such subjects as capital expenditure, the necessary money required to be voted by Parliament annually for operation, the question of the re-valuation of some of the roads, the elimination of particular services, and the closing down, temporarily, perhaps, of certain sections of railway.
I do not say that this committee should formulate and attempt to dictate policy to the Government, to Parliament, or to the country. All I urge is that it should be the instrument for disclosing full information that is much needed, all of which would go to inform Parliament, to educate the country, and thus gradually to evolve a sound public policy. The other day a motion was made by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), in which it was suggested that a complete disclosure of all information should be made to Parliament. As I said on that occasion, it may be that there was much to be said against that motion. It might well be a fair matter to commit to this committee the task of working out some other method of giving to Parliament all important or necessary information and thus perhaps avoiding a needless waste of time, at the same time giving to every one whatever was really necessary. The objection has been urged upon me privately that this matter should be referred to a special committee and not to a standing committee. I am not irrevocable in my judgment upon this. I am not particularly wedded to a standing committee in preference to a select committee, but I wish to point out that this will be a standing issue for some years. I think there will be much that a committee might do for more than one session, and more than the lifetime of

this Parliament, and I believe, therefore, that it will be better that this vast subject, in so far as it is to be treated by parliamentary committees, be referred preferably to a standing committee rather than a select or special committee.
A reference of the issue to a special committee at the present moment would, I fear, develop contests and antagonisms, that would not promote really useful and informative inquiry into the railway question; the very suggestion of a special committee suggests a contest. It has also been suggested that the present railway committee would suffice for my purposes. In answer to that suggestion I say that committee is too large, and its history and traditions are against useful work, particularly of the nature that I have outlined as being proper work for this committee. It has been urged, I think by the leader of the Opposition, that this committee should only inquire into such matters as were referred to it by the Government. There may be something in that contention, but its accuracy could only be developed later. I should think that if this committee were appointed, there is very little that it might not inquire into. I would hope that it being a parliamentary committee, and not a government committee,- the House from time to time would exercise the power vested in it and refer to that committee anything which it desired to refer. I wish again to impress upon the House the fact that I desire this committee to be a parliamentary committee, not necessarily a committee for Government purposes.
It has also been intimated to me that the management of the National Railway system would object to the constitution of this committee. I can hardly understand such opposition coming from the management. I can hardly understand the mentality of responsible men who, in view of the general situation, would take that position. I am not sure that that is their view. If it is I can only say that in my judgment they lack a clear apprehension of the great task that is ahead of them and now before then. Does the Government imagine for one single moment that it can get this country committed to the policy of government ownership and government control for twenty-four months, or for twelve months, unless there is some method of keeping the country informed from time to time upon the issue? In prosperous days, with a railway earning its operating expenses and building up reserves, the public probably would be quiescent in the matter, and it
would take very little to satisfy them; but I want to tell my right hon. friend who leads the Government that his credulity is almost laughable if he thinks that the country will permit him to conduct the National Railway system under its present policy-and I am not at the moment criticizing it-with the vast amount of taxation that must be imposed upon the people, unless he creates some avenues by which the people can be informed, by which the management and the public can be kept in touch with each other, and by which Parliament may know, as much as anybody else, about this question. If the management of the railway think that they can perpetuate themselves there, and at the same time carry on their duties in the background, without any means of seeking public approval of their policies and administration from time to time, and keeping that public informed, then I say it is very evident indeed they do not understand the problem which confronts them and the seriousness of the railway situation. I venture the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that if the chief officers of the Canadian National railways were to appear before a parliamentary committee for about ten days during a session of Parliament they would do more to establish themselves with the public than they can do by any other means to which they may resort to inspire or to obtain public confidence. I do not mean, Mr. Speaker, that this committee should engage in an inquiry into, and a discussion upon, all the trivial details of railway operation. I can quite understand you could not get a capable and intelligent railway manager to head the management of any railway system, particularly of a large system like this, if he were to be the subject of daily discussion in Parliament and of attack, even before a parliamentary committee, upon small trifling matters; it is very desirable that we abstain from criticism of that nature. What I seek to do, is\ to afford the opportunity for the manage- !) ment meeting a committee of the Parliament of Canada who represent the people so that, sitting together, they might discuss all the important matters relating to the railway administration, and I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that only through a parliamentary committee can this be done.
I want to say further, Mr. Speaker, that I doubt very much if the opinion of the railway management is as has been represented.
I know it is not the opinion of all the important officers of the management. I do know that it is not the judgment of all the

nominated directors of the National system. I know that many of them feel that their position is absolutely untenable, and that the whole situation will break down unless some method is provided of bringing the management into contact with the public, unless some method be devised of putting the public into a sort of relationship with the management such as shareholders are in annually with the management of ordinary commercial concerns. I take very little stock, Mr. Speaker, in the suggestion that has been made to me several times that he management are against the proposal for a parliamentary committee. It is an untenable position to take, and I venture to prophesy that after the experience of one week before a parliamentary committee they would abandon that foolish position, if, at the present moment, they entertain it at all. But whether they do or not I say that if the management want to have the support of the public, and they do want the support of the public, some such proposal as this one of mine is necessary. There is no management alive to-day, no management procurable by the Government, which can manage a railway system unless it has the support, of a section at least, of public opinion, and it must also have the support of Parliament, or at least a very large section of it. Otherwise it would be absurd to occupy the time of hon. gentlemen in seeking to establish the possibility of its continuance.
I admit, Mr. Speaker, that my suggestion perhaps contemplates a commitment of powers to a parliamentary committee far greater than we have hitherto witnessed. I know that the British system of parliamentary government strongly maintains the principle that all power and responsibility rests with the government. That was strongly asserted several years ago, and text book writers have affirmed that principle throughout the years in any discussion upon the British system of parliamentary government. But it is true that in actual practice, even in Great Britain, very important matters are now being committed to parliamentary committees, and splendid work has been done by them. In the United States splendid work was done last year by the Senate committee, particularly in the preparation of what is now the United States Transportation Act of 1920-the Act which transferred the control of the railway systems from the Federal Control Act to the Act which I have just mentioned. As I say, splendid work was done there, and a peru-

sal of the prolonged inquiry of the Senate committee would repay almost anybody, because the problems with respect to railways in the United States were very much the same as they are in this country. If there is any other possible way of bringing about a connection between an interested tax-paying and share-holding public, and it is better than this parliamentary committee and more likely to secure the results we seek, I should very gladly accept the suggestion.
Just one word in reference to the size of the committee which, I understand, the Prime Minister has intimated that he will appoint. It seems to me that that committee should not be a very large one; at the same time, I do not think it should be a very small one. It may be presumptuous on my part to make any suggestions in the matter at all, but inasmuch as I have perhaps made some astounding suggestions- at least, the Prime Minister may think I have-I might add just one more to the list without increasing the enormity of my offence. There is no doubt in my mind that if the operation of our railways is to continue under what is now virtually Government direction, with little prospect of any extensive construction during the next year or two, indeed, with a paring down of maintenance to the very limit, interprovincial jealousies will develop. Already instances have been observable in the press. I mean that when services are being curtailed, when sections of railway perhaps are to be abandoned temporarily or permanently, there is a natural tendency among persons living in the localities affected to believe that the railway management or possibly the Government are acting in a partial way. Therefore, if the Prime Minister will permit me, I would suggest that the committee should number about twenty-five or thirty-five members, and that in its constitution some respect should be paid to provincial representation.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that I have detained the House so long in presenting this matter, although I do not wish hon. members to think that I have exhausted the arguments that can be advanced in support of my motion. In fact, I doubt if I have given to the House the strongest reasons for the appointment of such a committee. However, I trust I have given such reasons as will induce the Government and the House to accept the suggestion which my motion contains. I move:

"Rule 10 of the House of Commons, relating to the appointment of the Select Standing Committees of the House, be amended for the present session by adding to the Select Standing Committees of the House for the present session a Select Standing Ooimimittee on Railways and Shipping owned, operated or controlled by the Government,1ifamd that the Special Committee appointed to'prepare and report the list of members to constitute the Standing Committees for the present session, be instruct. ed to prepare and report the list of members to compose the Select Standing Committee on [DOT]Railways and Shipping owned, operated or i controlled hy the Government' for the present j session."
