I should like to asic
my right hon. friend one or two questions before commenting on what he has said. Would he regard it as appropriate that there should be referred to the committee to which he 'has made reference the report of the Board of Directors-that the committee might consider any matter that is dealt with in that report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
I would consider it
right that the report of the Board of Directors should be referred to the committee. The committee, of course, would consider it for the purpose of giving a decision on the subjects referred to it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: What I am anxious to know is whether my right hon. friend thinks it would be proper for the committee to ask for information with respect to any matters that were suggested by that report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
Certainly, with a view
to determining its decision on the duties committed to it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
I am not
concerned about the committee's powers to determine what its duties will be. The point I am after is the power of the committee to secure information, facts, and answers to questions. Now, the report of the Board of Directors would deal with a number of matters pertaining to railway management, control, and operation, and it would naturally suggest a number of questions. What I should like to know is this: Would that committee have the power to get from the management answers to any questions which its members might wish to put with respect to any of these matters?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is not concerned with the duties of the committee, I am afraid there is not very much purpose in his question. The committee would necessarily direct all its efforts to the performance of its duties, and if it considered that any facts as to management were essential to enable it to determine these questions, it would have it within its powers to demand those facts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I am afraid that the replies of my right hon. friend are somewhat vague and evasive.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I will not say I think he purposely wishes them to be so, but if I understand the tenour of his remarks, they mean that this is a committee essentially for the study of what powers a body of the kind should have. I desire to know whether or not I am right in viewing the remarks of my right hon. friend in that way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: It is not a committee for the study of what powers it should have. That is only one question. I very clearly outlined four. The committee would be entitled to any information which it thought was necessary in order to enable it to come to a decision. I cannot answer more clearly than that, and, as we are not in committee, I think we should proceed with the debate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
I am prepared to proceed with the debate. Permit me, Mr. Speaker, to remind the House that the circumstance which occasioned this particular debate was a motion which was
introduced a few days ago on going into Supply, in which we on this side of the House asked the Government to supply Parliament with information with respect to matters pertaining to the operation, management, and control of the Canadian National Railways; averring in this connection that the Government should be responsible to Parliament in the giving of information and accounting for public expenditures, so far as the Canadian National Railways and the Railway Department are concerned, in the same way as in respect to any department of government. We were told at the time that it was impossible for the Government to give us information in answer to questions asked in Parliament, and further, that it was impossible for the Government to give information by way of orders for the production of papers and documents asked for. Speaking broadly, there are only three possible avenues whereby Parliament can be informed with regard to the administration of public matters: one, answers to questions asked of the ministry; another, the production of papers; and the third, through some committee of Parliament which has power to obtain information and report upon the same to Parliament.
Having been denied the first two sources of information, we naturally expected, when my hon. friend, the member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), had upon the Order Paper a resolution to the effect that Rule 10 of the House should be amended so as to establish a Select Standing Committee on Railways and Shipping, and when it was intimated by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), that in all probability the Government would accept something at least equivalent to what the hon. member had proposed, that we were to have at least one avenue whereby it would be possible for the people's representatives in Parliament to receive information in regard to matters appertaining to the control, operation and management of the Canadian National Railways. Instead of that, after listening to my right hon. friend this evening, we are now led to believe that all that the Government proposes is to appoint a committee for the purpose of studying and determining, for recommendation to Parliament, certain questions. That is an entirely different proposal from the one in which we are interested. What this Parliament wishes to obtain is information that will enable the public to understand, among other

things, how it is that a deficit occurred the year before last of ,$48,000,000 on these railways under Government management; how it is that that deficit was $70,000,000 Lor the past year; and how it is that in all probability it will be $100,000,000 for the present year. These are vast sums of public money which the people of the country have to provide by way of taxation, and the people will demand that the Government, in one form or another, shall he responsible for the accounting of every cent so spent, no matter whether it is paid out under some Board of Directors which the Government themselves may constitute, or paid out by a Government department direct.
Allow me Mr. Speaker, to draw the attention of the House to an important fact: Last year, when my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, made his statement to Parliament and announced, with surprise at that time, the enormous deficit of $48,000,000, we on this side naturally immediately asked for information that would help to explain that deficit. My hon. friend was quick in assuring us that as soon as the report of the Board of Directors of the National Railways was laid on the Table of Parliament we should be given ample powers of investigation in order to obtain all the information that was wanted. The hon. gentleman who sits beside him, the then Minister of Immigration and Colonization, the present President of the Privy Council (Mr. Calder), was also promptly on his feet to explain that the Government were anxious to get the Estimates through and that if we would only wait in our requests for information until the report of the Board of Directors were tabled, we could have all the committees we liked and the fullest investigation into the affairs of the railways. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister himself gave the House a definite assurance, in positive terms, that we could have all the information we desired in regard to matters appertaining to the report of the Board of Directors or to any other question concerning the operation, management or control of the national railways. Now, this year, when we have a deficit of $70,000,000, the Government changes its policy entirely, turns in a directly opposite direction, and informs us that we shall have no information whatever. They say: "We will give no information to the public by means of answers to question, or through the production of papers. We will not allow a special committee of Parliament to get that {Mr. Mackenzie King.]
information; all we will do is to concede a committee of Parliament for the purpose of studying certain academic questions"-questions which my right hon. friend has elaborated at great length-" but we will not give the committee power to get facts with respect to the cost of materials, with respect to contracts, with respect to methods of management; in other words, we will give no information that will help to explain this enormous deficit." Now, that is a position which, in the sight of the people of this country, is absolutely indefensible.
Let me make clear the distinction between the Government's present attitude and their professed attitude of last year. I do not say that it was their true attitude, because, as circumstances proved, once the Government got under way with the Estimates, they quickly forgot their promises that Parliament would be amply supplied with whatever information was required. In Hansard, on April 26, 1920, as reported at page 1671, will be found the following questions I addressed to my right hon. friend.
Mr. Mackenzie King:	The Minister of
the Interior said-and his remark was very significant

that while the Government would bring down a report somewhat in the nature of the report made by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, Parliament or any committee of Parliament would have a right to investigate everything disclosed by that report. I think I have reported my hon. friend correctly i-n that regard.
Mr. Meighen: That is right.
Mr. Mackenzie King: But what about the things that are not disclosed in that report? That is just exactly what we want to get at through the questions we are asking.
Mr. Meighen: If they have to do with the company, the hon. gentleman will have a right to information as to those also.
There is a statement which my right hon. friend made last year to this parliament. In regard to anything that had to do with the company, we on this side of the House, or members of Parliament generally, were to have right to the fullest possible information; but the doctrine laid down by my right hon. friend this year is that touching anything that appertains to the company we shall get no information. Only on such matters as relate to the department, and the relations between the department and contractors, for example, is this House to receive any information. Now, Mr. Speaker, we cannot bear too clearly in mind this complete change of front on the part of the Administration. This year they have brought forward a distinction, between the company's respon-


sibility in managing the railways and the Government's responsibility. They say that so far as the Government is concerned they have no responsibility other than as regards matters of a purely departmental concern; that anything pertaining to the management of the road through the company is something that concerns the company, and that Parliament is not to be informed upon it.
But the Prime Minister was not the only member of the Government who gave the assurance that if we passed the Estimates we would be supplied with any information as to the affairs of the company. His colleagues, in the House, as I have already mentioned, were all of one mind on that point. On April 26, 1920, the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) as reported on page 1671 of Hansard, said:
Every opportunity and every facility should be provided to this House to examine into every transaction. Everything that the management do may be brought under review.
Now we are told that nothing the management does is to be brought under review -the direct opposite. Again on page 1672 of Hansard my hon. friend is reported as follows:
This House will have the fullest opportunity to inquire into every dollar's worth of expenditure that has been made by the National railways during the past year.
Let me read the statement again, Mr. Speaker, and contrast it with the position which hon. gentlemen opposite are taking this year. Mark this: the statement was made at a time when the deficit was forty millions. We have now a deficit of seventy millions, and it is threatening to become a deficit of one hundred millions for next year. When the deficit was forty millions my hon. friend said:
This House will have the fullest opportunity to inquire into every dollar's worth of expenditure that has been made by the National railways during the past year.
More than that, the Minister of Immigration and Colonization went on to say:
It simply means that there will be a time when the fullest opportunity will be presented to Parliament to inquire into every detail of the work of the Canadian National Railway system.	.
There we have three distinct statements and pledges: first, that everything relating to the management shall be disclosed; second, that every dollar's worth of expenditure shall be accounted for; third, that every detail of the work may be inquired into. And now we are told by hon. gentlemen opposite that neither as respects the management nor the expenditure nor details of the work are the members of this Parliament to have any information whatever.
But the hon. ministers I have just quoted were not the only members of the Government who spoke in this way. I see opposite me the hon the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) and he, I think, will recall that he made a statement to the House at that time, as Minister of Finance, with respect to the attitude of the Government in giving information. That statement was made on April 26, 1920, and will be found at page 1680 of Hansard. It is as follows:
The House will be given the fullest opportunity to examine the report when it is brought down. Select committees or any thing else you like. These committees will be a great deal more than the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific will get, but make thorough inquiry then if you will, so long as the detailed business from day to day is not of necessity more or less interrupted.
In other words, what the Minister of Finance assured us was that so long as we did not question the ministry from day to day with respect to matters which might affect the business management of the system, that if we would be content to wait until the report was brought down, we could ask for committees and those committees would get all the information that they might want on any question that they liked to ask. Now we are told that we cannot have a committee except for the purpose of an academic inquiry.
But, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Railways also gave a pledge on behalf of the Government.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
You can rely on that
one.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
Here is the
pledge given by the Minister of Railways on June 25, 1920. It is to be found on page 4194 of Hansard and is as follows:
I would think that in the future there would be no reason why a special committee of the House should not be appointed i.n connection; with railways and let some of the officials come and explain the operations and give any information the committee may want.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what are we to conclude concerning the attitude of the Government at the present time when we have had the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Railways and other of their colleagues assuring Parlia-

ment before the Estimates are passed, that committees will be granted, that the fullest information will be conceded, that the House will get all the information it wants, and, then after the Government have succeeded in getting their Estimates through, they come hack to Parliament the next year and tell us that we will get information in regard to any of these matters one way or the other?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
Let me say,
Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada have a right to an accounting for every single dollar of public money that is being spent on the national system of railways, and no fiction, no subterfuge, on the part of my right hon. friend or his Government will serve as an excuse for that fundamental principle of responsible government not being adhered to if it is at all possible. What does my right hon. friend, or the Minister of Railways, say when we now ask them for information in regard to these roads? They say the Government has no responsibility; that responsibility belongs to the management. When we ask of the management theysay "We have noi responsibility, we are under the Board of Directors." At other times my hon. friends opposite also say to us "The Board of Directors are responsible." I think my right hon. friend said the other day that in this respect the Act would speak for itself. He disclaimed that any department of the Government was responsible and insinuated, though he did not say it, that by this Act, Parliament had made the Board of Directors responsible. Well, Mr. Speaker, let me read what the Act says in regard to the responsibility of the Board of Directors. It will be found in section 6 of the Statute 9-10 Geo. V., Chapter 13:
6. No Director of the Company shall be under any personal responsibility to any shareholder, director, officer or employee of the Company, nor to any other person, nor, except with the approval of the Governor in Council, shall be subject to any pecuniary penalty under the provisions of any statute, in Tespect of his office, or any act done or omitted to be done by him in the execution thereof.
In other words the Government virtually say "We will accept no responsibility," the Board of Management have no responsibility and the directors according to the Statute have no responsibility: in this way there are hundreds of millions of dollars of public money being spent with-
JTMr. Mackenzie King.l
out any responsibility one way or the other. My right hon. friend asks me: what is the explanation of the condition into which these roads have got; what is the explanation of this large deficit? It does not require any genius to make an answer or to give the explanation. Tell any man with hundreds and thousands of dollars to spend that he has no responsibility, that there is no responsibility in any direction, and you will very soon find money being squandered in all sorts of foolish directions -there is the explanation. We have departed from the fundamental principle of responsible government in the matter of holding the executive responsible for all expenditures of public moneys, and the minute you depart from that fundamental principle of government you bring the whole edifice to the ground. So, Mr. Speaker, the position we on this side take is that nothing will be satisfactory to the people of Canada except a return to the recognition of the obligation of the Government to account to the public for every cent of public expenditure. We will hold the Government responsible for the expenditure on these railways, and we will expect the ministry to find some way of giving Parliament the information which it has a right to have. Now I shall wait until we see what are "the concrete terms" -to use the words of my right hon. friend -in complete form which he suggests as to the means he proposes to give Parliament for securing information before stating what further action we will take. But I would tell my right hon. friend now that if he brings in a motion at all in accord with the statement which he made this evening, if he brings along the suggestion of a committee with only the right to study and report, it will not be acceptable to the people of this country and will be strongly opposed by those of us on this side of the House. We will not oppose it for the sake of offering any opposition to a committee. What we will demand is a committee with powers sufficiently wide to get information which the people have a right to be supplied with in view of the very serious condition that this problem has brought the country face to face with at the present time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
What about the large
details?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
With regard to the
large details, the committee that it is proposed to create is asked to report to us as to what the information is that this House can be given, and, consequently, should be given consistently with the two public interests that I have pointed out, to report to us what is the best method of obtaining that information and of giving it to the House in view of the purpose of conciliating these two public interests; then to report to us upon the system of auditing that should be adopted and the extent of detail that should be given in the annual report, this for the purpose of enabling the House to decide what information should be obtained in the public interest and what is the best method of obtaining it; and, finally, whether and for what purposes the committee should be continued. Now, it is not proposed that this committee shall be the method of obtaining information for the general purposes of this House. If it were so, how illogical it would be on the part of this House-and that is what I understand the leader of the Opposition suggests ought to be done-having first decided that there should be some discrimination with regard to the information which the House should ask for and obtain, to proceed to appoint a committee that would exercise no discrimination whatever, but ask for anything and everything that any member of that committee might want. The hon. gentleman entirely misapprehends the proposal that has been put forward here. What the House is asked to do is to ascertain what is the best instrument whereby the information

that we ought to get can be obtained, and, through its committee, to state, having regard to the consideraions I have mentioned, what information ought to be made public. Then, there is the question of the best method of obtaining that information, and, finally, the best method of auditing the accounts of these different companies, so that the reports of the auditors may be accepted as statements of the proper condition of the companies in which we are interested. Last of all, there is the question of the permanency of the committee.
Now, save when he thinks it is necessary for oratorical purposes to work himself up into apparently uncontrollable indignation, the leader of the Opposition, I believe, earnestly desires to find a method by which he may consistently with the public interest get that information for which he so hungers and thirsts. All that this House is asked to do is to provide a committee to report to this House as to what is the best method of attaining that desirable end. Is that not a reasonable proposal? Surely the debate of the other day made it quite clear that two conflicting principles required to be conciliated if the public interest was to be served. And what is the present proposal? That we sit down and study with the aid of a committee what is the best way to conciliate those two principles so as effectively to serve the public interest. I am sure that any one who reflects for a moment will see how entirely uncalled for was the wrathful indignation of the hon. leader of the Opposition and will recognize in this suggestion a sincere desire to arrive at a practical method of finding a solution of the difficulties:; that present themselves and of achieving the necessary result of providing the House with the information to which it is entitled and of so nroviding it as not to bring about any deteriment to the public interest.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria) :
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unless we are entirely mistaken in the purposes of Parliament and in the constitutional rights of the people of this country, the representatives of the people have some purpose in coming here. Otherwise we on this side, acting under some illusion and under "indignation" as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) says, completely misapprehend the purpose of our coming here. Are we not to know'anything at all? Are we not to ask any questions for conscience' sake? Are we to submit tamely to everything that the Minister of Justice passes out to us?
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that that is the TMr. Doherty.]
purpose of the people of this country in sending us here, notwithstanding the lessons and reprimands which come to us from the Department of Justice. We on this side, while never over-satisfied with the analytical disquisitions of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) always manage to understand pretty well what he means. He told us very clearly to-night what was intended by this commiteee. But the Minister of Justice was not satisfied with the English language as presented by the Prime Minister. He thought it was a jumble of words without meaning; that indignation was possibly provoked by their presentation, and, as a Daniel come to judgment, the Minister of Justice, in his lucid, clear-cut, well-determined sentences, told us exactly what the Prime Minister meant. The hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) took high ground when he said that there really was nothing to the purpose in the speech of the right hon. Prime Minister. If there was any doubt as to the soundness of the position taken by the leader of the Opposition we have the most conclusive proof of its correctness in the commentary of the Minister of Justice.
Let me remind the Minister of Justice of what he said a very few seconds after he got through with his speech. He said: "The leader of the Opposition works himself into a fury of indignation, of wrath, over imaginary difficulties." That is his language. As a humble representative of the people of this country, I ask the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice if a deficit of $49,000,000 last year in the operation of a public utility with which the people have to do, where the people have to furnish the money to pay every cent of that expenditure, where the freight rates of the country were raised 40 per cent over and above what they used to be, where enormous amounts of money have been dragged and extorted out of the pockets of the people of Canada for keeping this incubus going-I ask them if that was an imaginary thing. Yet, after this was all done and additional millions of dollars were filched out of the pockets of the people, the Government come back and tell us: "Last year we had a simple deficit of $49,000,000 which, in the estimation of so worthy a gentleman as the right hon. Minister of Justice, is a mere illusionary matter that no person should be concerned about; it is imaginary and not worth asking any questions about at all." I see a number of able business men sitting around and behind the Government. I should like

to ask them if, when they go hack to their constituencies in all parts of the country, they are asked: "What is the condition of the railways; I am told that last year you had a deficit of $49,000,000; that this year you have a deficit of $70,000,000, and that next year you will have a deficit of $100,-000,000"-if they will undertake to wave their constituents aside and say: "Oh, gentlemen, do not be illusionized by these things; they are merely imaginary. All you have to do is to imagine that there is no such a thing as a Government railway at all. All you have to do is to imagine that the Government railways made $65,000,000 of profit last year, and you have the money in your pocket." So the Minister of Justice says. I told the right hon. gentleman once before that we in the province from which I come are in the habit of having the greatest respect for the office and the person of the Minister of Justice, and I would feel myself rather confused if a man stood up and produced this Hansard at a public meeting, say in the town of Sydney Mines and said: "Why, you are talking about deficits; the right hon. Minister of Justice said last year that that was merely imaginary; that there was no such a thing at all." Will the right hon. gentleman say that that is really the fact?
I submit this to the usually fair mind of the Minister of Justice. It has been proven to the hilt that last year, before the Estimates were through, before we gave the money to Parliament and to the Government to spend, we were promised by one minister after another, by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) by the then Minister of the Interior, by the then Prime Minister himself and, I am sure, by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Bal-lantyne), who is usually prolific in promises and very barren in performances, that every dollar that was expended of the money of the public would be accounted for. I am sure the Minister of Marine and Fisheries told us that every dollar of the public money spent in his department would be accounted for twice over. Those were the promises. Did hon. gentlemen expect members of the House and, in particular, members of the Opposition to believe them? I am sure they will not dare to say in this House: "We made those statements, but we did not expect you to believe them. We were not sincere." I am sure they will not dare to take that attitude. We believed them; we voted the money, and here we are this year with all this money expended and $70,000,000 more expended that we did
not vote at all. The Government come back to us now in face of those promises, and the Minister of Justice, leading the van, says: "You will not get one word, not one iota, not one figure; you can just go and do your best about the matter; we will sit tight here, and you will not know one thing that is going on behind our closed doors; we are in the dark lantern brigade which you said we were in, and we will not flinch one inch from the position we take." Does the right hon. gentleman not think that is a subject for indignation, if there was indignation? Does he not think that is a reason why the people of this country should rise in their might and say: "What is the good of Parliamentary representation? What is the good of having the name of responsible government if these facts are not given to the people." I can only repeat what the hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition says, and I think it is plain and simple. We still adhere to the doctrine of responsible Government, to the position that the minister of every department of Government must come down to this House and explain its expenditure. I do not think, when the business of this country is carried on under twenty departmental heads, we can say that they are overburdened and overloaded with work when we ask them to be able to come down to this Parliament and explain in reasonable detail what has become of the money of the country. If the Department of Railways has become top-heavy, if it is too big, if it cannot be handled by one man, why not divide the work up so that departments which have not so much to do will have some part of that work and give us details which are necessary in order to satisfy the people of Canada that their moneys are properly expended? I remember when we sat behind the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier as Premier of this country and hon. gentlemen who are to-day on your right, Sir, were on this side of the House, we had to account for every dollar, and if a few thousand dollars were expended by way of ever-expenditure or anything of that kind, the greatest possible storm was raised until every dollar was accounted for. That was the proper thing. When a change of Government took place, when those hon. gentlemen went to your right, and when they have the purse-strings and the expenditure of the money of this country, is there any doctrine that can be thought of for one moment but that for every farthing of the money which they

expend, they shall account to the honest people of this country who are furnishing the cash and who have, for the time being, given the Government their confidence in the expenditure of that money? There is only one doctrine, one position, one stand that any sane community or representative can take in this House or in the country.
As regards the idea of appointing this committee, have we not enough committees already? I have not said anything so far about this committee; I do not care very much whether it is appointed or not. We have already a string of standing committees, and why should this public business not be sent to one of them? Every dollar that we are going to have inquired into before this committee is money belonging to public account, is it not? We have a Public Accounts Committee. If there is anything to be inquired into by way of the public accounts of this country, why does it not go to the Public Accounts Committee? Is that not what a Public Accounts Committee is for?- Is there any money expended in connection with the ships, the railways, the Post Office, Public Works or any other department that is handled by the Government that is not public money? Therefore, if the Government desires a full inquiry into this question, should it not be sent to the Public Accounts Committee? It is not the function of any committee to do the business of the Government. If there is any inquiry which members of Parliament may require; if they are dissatisfied with any account that the Government has brought down, they may ask for a committee. But in the first instance it is the duty of the Government to be prepared to give every information that may be required, and if details are asked for by people who may be dissatisfied, then the question may go to a committee for a further investigation. But the floor of Parliament, and not a committee, is the place for hon. members to find out the facts. The idea of saying that there are no politics in the management of the road; that it is entirely free from politics, and then after all is said and done and you come to an inquiry and an investigation, the matter is to be sent to a partisan, political committee, because in this House you cannot get a committee other than a partison committee that will act in a partisan manner. I have been on quite a number of committees, and when a matter came to the test, I never saw anything but a clear-cut division on the partisan bias of each member of the com-
mittee, and that is what would happen in this case.
I submit therefore that instead the right hon. Minister of Justice should have devoted himself to answering the charges that were made by the leader of the Opposition, that promises were made last year to give this information, and that the information is not only not forthcoming now, but has been absolutely denied. The Minister of Justice tells us that the business of this committee is to perform the impossible. He tells us that its business is to provide intelligence for the Department of Railways, intelligence and wisdom for the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and efficiency for the management of our railways. If he can find a committee under God's blue canopy that will give intelligence to the Department of Railways, wisdom to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and efficiency and executive ability to the railway management, I should certainly like to see the personnel of that committee.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact that apparently I am particularly to blame in connection with the promise said to have been made last year-and I have no doubt it was made-impels me to throw myself very unexpectedly into this debate. But once in it, I think that we should all try: to understand at the earliest possible moment that we are debating a very serious situation, a very serious question of policy and of principle.
It is easy to say "losses"; it is easy to say that public ownership is wrong; it is easy to throw the cheap gibe and the cheaper sneer. We are told that last year we only asked for so many millions, and that under public ownership this
11 p.m. year we are asking an enormously increased vote. I would like to point out one thing to hon. gentlemen, for we might just as well get down to the basis, and see whether their basis is right; they may be right by accident.
I would point out that the tremendously increased vote this year is not the result of public ownership; it is not the result of anything that has been done by the committee now managing the national railways. The tremendous vote this year is the result very largely of private operation, private ownership and private management of the Grand Trunk Railway. We are asking a vote this year of $87,000,000 for the Grand Trunk itself, run and operated as a private company. Now, there is a

great deal of room for debate as to whether or not the people as a people can properly run, own and operate a railway, but there is no room for debate on one phase of that question, for it has been settled by every country that has tried it, and that is you cannot run a difficult, complex business organization such as a railway, covering an enormous mileage and touching the home life of the people in every city and town the whole country over, by direct parliamentary control. I do not think there is any room for debate on that question, and if there be no room for debate on that question, it seems to me we are perhaps not arguing the real point at issue, that point being whether or not public utilities can be operated through commission form or by trustees for the public in the interests of the public. That is really what we are arguing to-day. We are not arguing anything else. I put it to any hon. gentleman who has studied public ownership of public utilities by direct parliamentary control; has he ever found it result in anything except absolute failure?

Will ]my hon. friend
tell me whether under our system he could have any control if he had not parliamentary control. He either must have parliamentary control or no control at all. The people are responsible. My hon. friend cannot get away from that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
That is a
perfectly proper question, and I shall be very pleased to deal with it. As I was saying the issue here is really whether or not public ownership as we understand it, public operation as we hope to get it, is to be given a fair trial. I want to touch just for a moment on the point raised by my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill). I think there is a great deal of difference between bringing up all the little details
of management, the small questions which inevitably always are, and always must be, questions for immediate and prompt decision by the management, and the larger and more important questions which arise out of the results of the management's operation and out of their annual report. Now last year-I am going to try and be consistent, and I think I am-

You will find it very
hard.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
Not as yet.
I would find it very hard to reach the heights of fancy and joke that my hon. friend can, but so far I have not found it very hard to be consistent. Last year I said that I saw no reason why the report of the directors should not be dealt with by a committee. I conceive that to be a very different thing from worrying the management day in and day out for information as to the petty details of management. I am quite sure hon. gentlemen know very well how railways are run, and that I shall only be drawing to their attention something they know all about when I say that the function of a railway president is really the function of giving prompt and just business decisions. He is a referee of tremendous responsibility. He must dispose of an infinitude of questions in a very short time if he is to deal effectively with them, and for the iife of him he could not tell you, a month after a decision was given, why he had done this or that in connection with some small matter of detail. The leader of the Opposition stated that there was no responsibility on the part of the directors. Well, I am sure my hon. friend wants to be fair, and he will find that the provision that is there made in the statute is one which is incorporated in many and many an Act for a public purpose, where duties are cast upon individuals who do not directly share in the profits of an enterprise. All that is stated there is that the directors shall not be personally responsible in damages for acts done in their capacity as directors, and you have that provision also in connection with the managers of many companies. It does not mean that they are not responsible for their management; they are responsible therefor just as much as any hon. gentleman is responsible to his constituents for what he does in Parliament. Now, if there be any better way, we ought to try-to find it; and, after all, that is what we are trying to do.
