speechtext: Through what channel?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Through this House.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: And they have made their reports accordingly.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: There are no details.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: The hon. member will find that there are complete details of everything that really goes to solve the question as to whether or not these men are efficient, and whether they are running this public enterprise properly. The yardsticks are all given. As a matter of statutory duty, these reports are filed every year. The full particulars of the different activities are all given,-passenger activities, freight, mails, express, and miscellaneous operations, together with operating expenses. They are all given, and if there be anything more that should be done, I would have thought that it would be done just as I suggested last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: To whom is their report addressed?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
The report
goes to the Minister of Railways and is by him tabled annually.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Then he is responsible?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
He simply
tables the report.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Can these directors be brought before the Public Accounts Committee for examination?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I do not know that there is any reason why they should not be. Of course, I know many reasons why in some respects this is not desirable.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: What are they?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: If many small matters of detail are to be inquired into; if they are to be asked to give up the full information regarding their traffic arrangements, for example; if they are to be asked to disclose' full information as to-

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: As to deficits.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I did not catch that.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I said, information as to deficits.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Oh, we will come to that later on. I was saying, if they are to be asked to disclose full information as to their business relations as directors in connection with their different industrial sidings; in other words, if they are to be asked to give up all that business information which every man in business for himself regards as his private property, and if they are to turn all this over to the advantage of a competitor, then there are many reasons why they should not appear before the committee for this purpose. On the other hand, if they are brought before a committee such as we now suggest, or any other committee, for the purpose of enquiring into their operations with a view to ascertaining whether economies could not be effected, and moneys saved in various ways, no reason in the world could be advanced against this. As to the deficit, that is certainly a matter that should be looked into. It is certainly a large operating result; it is certainly a matter about which very few persons can find anything for laughter; at least I cannot; it is certainly something which ought to be reduced, if possible.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Would not that be accomplished by going into the small details? Little drops of water make the mighty ocean.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
If the hon.
member started counting the drops of water in the ocean, he would not be engaged very much longer in the process than he would be in trying to find out exactly what was wrong with the railways by going into little bits of detail here and little bits there. By the time he got them all collected he would have such a mass of material that it would be absolutely impossible for him or any one else to digest it. That is undoubtedly something which any railway president, or any other man who understood the operations of railways, would regard as ridiculous. Do you think that a railway president looks after matters of detail? Do you think that any man charged with large affairs, carrying on an enormous business running into millions, bothers about details himself? He has many persons under him to look after these matters.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Suppose the appointment of an agent at some station might mean a clear profit of $15,000 a year to the railways, does not the minister think that1 an agent should be placed there?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I think that any one who was entrusted with the large responsibility of running the country's railways would he in a far better position to judge as to whether or not an agent should he put on at any particular station. That is something that is left in the hands of the management.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I was suggesting a case where a clear profit of $15,000 would accrue.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: If there is any case such as is suggested by the member, it is not necessary to make trouble either in the House or with the management. All he has to do is to go before the Board of Railway Commissioners.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: It is not under their control.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
They are
bound to appoint an agent where there are earnings of $15,000, not net but gross. The hon. gentleman is wrong; the lines are under the board. The board fix their rates, and while the statute does not give them, as a board, the right to interfere in detail matters of operation, through letters of the ministers of railways the board have exercised that jurisdiction. Certainly the railway management will not refuse to appoint an agent where such an appointment is necessary.	>

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will allow me I can tell him that the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners says the contrary?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Well, I can only speak from recollection which is quite recent, as to the very general practice. I exercised the right and I exercised it at the request of the Government. But after all the Act is there and it will not be very long, I hope, before the anomaly is removed if the matter be in the position to which the hon. gentleman refers.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Would the minister consider the purchase of supplies and equipment a fair subject for inquiry by the committee?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
You would
have that in the report and everything that is in the report, I think, is a perfectly fair matter for inquiry.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Would we be free to ask for copies of tenders?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I do not think that is something that ought to be done. Let me tell the hon. gentleman something that we know about. Let me tell him that after would-be contractors, who were trying to get a specific price for commodities, had failed to secure a contract-that contract having been let to a lower tenderer-questions were asked in the House as to the details of those tenders. It is a dangerous thing to try and run a competitive business in such a way, where the men you want to do business with know exactly what they have got to bid and how near they come to the prices offered by their competitors. It is certainly not the way that any railway company in the world that has ever made a success of its business has been operated. After all, what are we trying to do? What we are trying to do is to see if we cannot better the present condition, see if we cannot compose the differences that exist. I think those differences are largely differences which can be easily composed, because I am quite confident that so soon as we realize what the effect on the country as a whole would be if there is indiscriminate searching from time to time and day to day into the business of this large concern, we are all going to be together. We are trying to see what is the best thing to be done. When I said last year-and there again the difference can be so easily illustrated-that there was no objection at all to the fullest reference of the report, or anything else that was asked, to a committee, is there not the greatest difference in the world between that and the asking of questions-for example, such a question as was put the other day in the House as to why an agent was not at work for a given number of hours in a particular city?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: My hon. friend has spoken of "the Board of Directors" of the Canadian National Railway. Has any board of directors been appointed under the law which was passed a few years ago? Has that corporation been organized to any extent at all, or are the railways managed, as they were then, under the Government by commissioners appointed by it?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: By order in council.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is quite correct to a certain extent; but I am afraid that in the main he is quite wrong. It is quite true to say that

the general Act has not yet been put into effect, but it is also entirely untrue to say that the railway system is governed by a commission. The Board of Directors are elected just in exactly the same way as the board of directors of any company would be elected.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Except there is only one shareholder.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Not by the shareholders.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Perhaps hon. gentlemen will allow me for one moment; I am now speaking in answer to a question. They are elected in exactly the same way as the directors of any other company; there is one difference and only one. That one difference is that instead of a certain portion of the public being interested in the election of the directors, the whole of the public are interested in it, and that instead of the shareholders-through their proxies as is usually done-electing -the directors, the whole of the people elect the directors through the Government.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :
maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance asked a question a few moments ago, a very proper question, "What are we trying to do?" I will not undertake to describe what I think my hon. friends opposite are trying to do; I did that the other day and they thought I was not as courteous as I ought to be. But I will undertake to tell my hon. friends, and the Government, what we on this side are trying to do. We are simply trying to assert and to maintain the right of the people of Canada to receive an accounting-in gross or in detail as they please-through their representatives of every dollar of the public money that is spent. That is what we are trying to do- only that and nothing more. But that is something which is so plain and so simple that I am satisfied the people of Canada will readily understand it. But hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to make excuses for not doing that, and they are raising men of straw in order that they may knock them down. They are raising ghosts as to all the difficulties in the way. "Why," says the Minister of Finance, "if all these little details were brought down here what a trouble it would be." Well, I will not repeat the argument I used the other day. Our contention is that this matter should be dealt with precisely in the same way as it would be in the case of one of our own departments; there is no reason why the same principle should not apply. If the Prime

Minister is going to move for a committee, and the proceeding will give to the House all the rights and privileges which it has as respects every other department of Government, that will be all right; but if he is going to say "We will give the House information regarding the Department of Public Works, but we will refuse it as regards the Canadian National Railways," I say that is wrong. We are going to stand on that and make that the issue in this House and if necessary before the country. The hon. gentleman, I say, raises a ghost for the purpose of trying to show that there are difficulties in the way. He says, "What good are these details anyway?" But take the position of the Department of Public Works or the Department of Railways, any or all of the departments of Government, and the way we act with respect to them. We have the right to demand the details as to every dollar of expenditure of the Public Works Department, but we do not do it. Why should we not have the same privilege as regards the national system of railways? We would have the right under our contention to deal with all these matters of detail, but we would not do it. Why? Because they are not necessary. To-day a question is asked regarding the Department of Public Works; in the matter of a contract for example, suppose a question is asked now about the price that is paid for coal? Well, the Minister of Public Works may reply, "I may say to the hon. gentleman that that matter is still under consideration. We have received tenders but we have not awarded contracts and we are not able to give the information"-a perfectly proper answer and the House would accept it. But if the same question is raised regarding the Canadian National Railways we are told, "That is a violation of all business rules," and we are not to know the price that the Government railway management paid for coal although we would be told what the Public Works Department paid for such a commodity. There is no earthly difference between the two. I suppose the Department of Public Works every year pays-I do not know the exact number but at a rough guess I would say ten thousand accounts. How many of them do we bring before Parliament? We do not bring them before Parliament once in a blue moon, unless something arises which calls for an investigation. We have the right to investigate every item, and we should have the right, but we do not exercise it. Why should we not have the same right in the case of the Government railways?

It is one thing to have the right to go into all these details, and in giving that right without any restriction or limitation you are carrying out the proper principles of parliamentary government; but when you deny and restrict that right; then you are departing from all the soundest principles of parliamentary government. I utterly fail to see any reason why we cannot apply to the railways of Canada the same principle that we apply to the public works or the marine and fisheries. I have not found any indication yet of any kind of information the bringing down of which could do harm to our railways. Not one of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken has given us an illustration of something we might ask for, but which the railway company might properly refuse to give. In a motion that we laid on the Table the other day we recognized the fact that at all times there are certain matters in connection with government which in the wisdom of the Government they may see fit to withhold. We recognized that fully, and we recognize it as fully in the matter of our railways as in the matter of the Marine and Fisheries or the Public Works departments. The Government have to be the judges of that, and the House will always recognize reasonable grounds refusing information of that character. What we on this side contend for is that the principle which applies to every other department of government should apply to the Canadian National railways. Not a shadow of ground has yet been shown to indicate that any harm would be done by bringing down any item of the information we have asked for. I take the illustration in regard to coal. I can understand that if we asked for information about tenders for coal the Minister of Railways would say: "This matter is under consideration, it is not settled, and the information cannot be brought down." But after the contract has been awarded, what earthly interest can suffer by the answering of a question as to what companies we got the coal from and what prices we paid for it? It is all nonsense to say that you are going to give information to your competitor, the Canadian Pacific railway. Your competitor certainly knows all there is to know in connection with railway matters. Do not be alarmed about the Canadian Pacific railway. The are pretty shrewd, wise fellows, and they know all that is of any value to know.
But the simple question I am answering is the question of the Minister of Finance. What we are trying to do, and what we are going to do with all our energy, whether we succeed or not, is to stand for the rights of the people of Canada to have either in gross or in detail whatever information may seem to be reasonably necessary in the judgment of any member of this House as respects the expenditure of every dollar of public money that the people of Canada are obliged to pay.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the discussion has arisen through the resolution of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) which asks that a special" committee be apointed to inquire into the operation of the national railways; in other words, to dig into the operation of those railways with a view to recommending any improvement that they can suggest with reference to that operation. As to the whole of the details being given to the House, I was one of those that sat at that time on the opposite side of the Government when the Canadian Northern railway was taken over, and I absolutely insisted that the railways should be put under the management of an independent commission in so far as it was pqssible to put them under such a commission, I believe that that has been done. I believe that the present Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) has carried out that policy to the fullest extent and that he has interfered as little as possible with the management.
Answering my right hon. friend who has just sat down, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), for whom I have the greatest respect, I remember last year when the discussion took place over the Minister of Railway's statement that the minister did not hesitate to give to the House any information in his power. I remember distinctly with reference to the question of coal that he gave the purchase price in the various sections of the country through which the railway operated. Nor do I think has this Government refused any reasonable request on the part of any member of the Opposition or on the part of any other hon. member with reference to the operation of our national railways. But you must bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that we insisted that those railways should be operated as far as possible by an independent commission. That is being done. You cannot bring those men on to the floor of the House to

illustrate every little detail with reference to the operation of the system, and it is not customary for any corporation to give such details to its shareholders. I have had a good deal of experience on boards of directors, and I have never yet known the shareholders to ask for absolute details of operation.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Why not?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Why not? Those details are open to them if they want to go and .examine the books.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
That is what
we want to know.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
I have no doubt that
-details of the management of the national railways are open to any member of the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
Have you tried and
have you been refused?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
The minister refuses
everything.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I do not believe anybody has been refused. Let me repeat, I do not know any corporation that tells its shareholders the details of its operations.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: We know.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I doubt if you do.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I do.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
As to this proposed committee of the House consisting of members on both sides as I understand it, the hon. member from North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) tonight said that on special committees partisan discussion was just as likely to arise as on the floor of the House. I have sat on special committees .appointed to discuss all kinds of questions since I have been in this House, and I will say for the Opposition, no matter which side of the House I sat on, that I never :saw a question debated by any of those special committees from a party standpoint. Take the question of soldiers' reestablishment, the committee on which sat for two months. I have only this to say for the hon. members who sat with me on that committee, members of the present Opposition, that never by any chance was there a word or action that would suggest that we were discussing the question from [DOT]a party standpoint. And the report was xnot brought in from a party standpoint.

Any spectator who attended the meetings of that committee would not have known which party the members belonged to as far as the discussion was concerned. Therefore I believe that great benefit would be derived by the appointment of a special committee to thoroughly investigate the question of the operation of these national railroads and to report back to the House.
Let me repeat, that I know of no instance where the Minister of Railways in discussing the annual statement of the national railways last year refused to give any information in his power, and I doubt if he will now. I think you are raising a mountain out of a molehill in discussing this question, because I believe that, after all, we all view the matter from the same standpoint, and I am as certain as I am that I am standing here that there will be no difficulty on the part of the Prime Minister in selecting from this side of the House, and on the part of the leader of the Opposition in selecting from that side of the House, men who will forget whether they are Liberals or National Liberal Conservatives, and who as soon as they are appointed on that committee will forget their party prejudices and do the best they can to work out a solution of this very serious question confronting the country at the present time. I hope that that will be the view of the men who are appointed on that committee, and I am quite sure from my past experience that it will be their view, and I hope the Prime Minister will carry out his intention of appointing such a committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) asked a question the reply to which is really an answer to the whole discussion. He said, as I understood him, we could not have public ownership cocurrently with parliamentary control; I think that is a fair repetition of what he said. Now, if that is the case, it will be impossible for us to have public ownership, because we will not give up parliamentary control. I am not an enemy of public ownership; ever since I came to this House, and before, I have been attracted to public ownership. I have been seeking further light on the question and honestly and anxiously inquiring how the matter worked out in practice. I must frankly admit that until now nearly all the evidence that has been brought before me has been against public control and pub-

lie operation of railways. But let me say this: we have to have control of railways, and that control has either to be responsible or irresponsible. I do not think that any member of this House will say for a moment that that control should be irresponsible. Then it must be responsible, and to whom? In the ultimate analysis, to the members of this House. And if you cannot have public ownership which involves ultimate responsibility to this House, then public ownership will have to be given up. .After all, public ownership is merely a matter of expediency. It may be wise or it may be unwise; it may be advantageous or it may be disadvantageous, but the control of the expenditure of public money by this House is a matter of principle, the very basis of our parliamentary institutions and of our British constitutional practice.
The gentlemen who have spoken on the other side have been.at great pains to point out the possible dangers of parliamentary control. They have set up the imaginary bogey that if this House inquires concerning different details of management the Canadian Pacific Railway company will catch on. I think I can say with a fair degree of assurance that nothing of substantial importance happens concerning any railroad in Canada or in the northern part of the United States of which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are ignorant. It is part of their business to know; I believe they know their business and are well advised as to what goes on with their competitors. After all, the operation of railways is not carried on in the dark, and it must be known what railways pay for their supplies just as the schedules are known upon which the trains are run. So far as rates are concerned they are fixed by a public board, and there is no possibility of one competitor hiding from another the details in that connection. But the point I wish to impress upon the House to-night is that the system of irresponsible control is one which may breed most unwholesome conditions in this country. I accuse no one of wrong-doing in the remarks which I propose to make to-night. But I say that the Government has placed the railways of this country in the hands of a small committee who are called directors but who are the creatures and nAninees of the Government, and that a large number of these men are directors in companies which, if not selling to the railways, have in hand the goods to sell to the railways. I also wish to make this point, Mr. Speaker: these men are directors not only in the Canadian Na-102
tional Railways but also in such a number of other companies as to preclude their giving to the railways of the country that care and attention which the railway situation demands. Now, the other day the member for Essex (Mr. Kennedy) asked the following questions in the House.
1.	What are the names of the gentlemen who compose the Board of Management of the Canadian National Railways?
2.	What is the salary of each and what amount did each receive as expenses during the past year?
3.	Are any of these gentlemen also directors of joint stock companies doing business in Canada?
4.	If so, of what company or companies are they respectively directors?
To which the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) made the following replies:
1.	D. B. Hanna, A. J. Mitchell, R. T. Riley, R. Hobson, Major G. A. Bell, Sir Hormisdas l.aporte. Col. Thomas Cantley, A. P. Barnhill, E. R. Wood.
2.	Director's fees, $2,000 each, and travelling expenses to and from their homes.
3.	The Government has no information.
4.	Answered by No. 3.
I would direct attention to the fact that the answer to number 2 was only a partial answer; the question, "what amount did each receive as expenses during the past year" was not answered, it being merely stated that they receive travelling expenses to and from their homes. Now, as a matter of elementary propriety and justice, the Canadian people, who are paying to Mr. Hanna $25,000 a year and to the other directors, who are not expected to give all their time to the consideration of railway matters, $2,000 a year and their travelling expenses, are entitled to know what other companies these directors are interested in, if for no other purpose than to know how far their attention is distracted from the railway problem which is in their special charge. As that information was withheld from the members of this House I examined the Financial Guide of 1920 and I discovered these facts, which I think, should be of interest to the House and perhaps of interest to the country. I find that Mr. D. B. Hanna, who, as I have said, receives $25,000 a year, if I mistake not, as manager of our Canadian National Railways, is also a director in the following companies: Canada Steamship Lines, Limited; Electrical Development Company of Canada, Limited; Canada Mortgage Investment Company; British-American Assurance Company; Western Assurance Company; Canadian North Prairie Lands Company; Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company, Limited; Rio de Janeiro Light and



Power Company; Sao Paulo Light and Power Company. He is also president of the Canada Flour Mills. Mr. A. J. Mitchell is a director in only one company, the Western Canada Flour Mills. Mr. R. T. Riley is interested as a director in but two companies. He is vice-president of the Union Bank of Canada and vice-president of the Great West Life Assurance Company. Mr. Robert Hobson is a director in the Bank of Hamilton; he is a director in the Canada Locomotive Company, Limited; he is president of the Steel Company of Canada, Limited; he is a director in the Tuckett Tobacco Company, Limited, in the North Star Oil and Refining Company, in the Chartered Trusts and Executor Company, in the British Empire Trust Company, in the Dominion Power and Transmission Company and in the Toronto General Trusts Corporation. Major G. A. Bell is, I understand, a civil servant, and so far as I can learn, he is a director in no company whatsoever. Sir Hormisdas Laporte is a director in the Credit Foncier Franco-Canadien, in the Societe d'Administration Generale, in the Frontenac Breweries Limited and in La Sauvegarde Life Assurance Company.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
He is president of
Laporte-Martin, Limited.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: What do they do?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: They sell wholesale groceries in Montreal.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: They do not sell liquor, do they?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
I do not know. They probably will not after the first of May. Col. Thomas Cantley is a director in the Eastern Car Company Limited, in Brand-ram-Henderson Paints and Varnishes and in the' Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, Limited. Mr. A. P. Barnhill is a director in the Eastern Trusts Company, in James Pender and Company, Limited, in the St. John Iron Works, Limited, and in the Telegraph Publishing Company. He is president of the New Brunswick Electrical Company. He is president of the Acamac Land Company, Limited. He is a director in the Fenton Land 12 m. and Building Company, in the Westfield Land Company, in the Times Publishing Company, and in the New Brunswick Realty Company. Last, but not least, in the number of directorships he holds is Mr. E. R. Wood, who is a director in the British American Assurance

Company, a vice-president of the Canada Life Assurance Company, a director in the Western Assurance Company, a director in the Canadian Bank of Commerce. One would have thought that the connection between that bank and the late lamented Canadian Northern railway wouild have been sufficient to have made the Government believe it was inadvisable to have a director of that bank connected with the railway lines of this country. He is a director in the Barcelona Traction, Light and Power Company, Limited; he is vicepresident of the Brazilian Traction, Light and Power Company, Limited; he is a director in the Rio de Janeiro Light and Power Company, in the Sao Paulo Tramway Light and Power Company, in the Mexico Tramways Company, in the Toronto Railway Company, in the Toronto Power Company, Limited, in the Toronto Electric Light Company, Limited, and in the Electrical Development Company of Canada, Limited. He is a vice-president of the National Trust Company and a director in the Dominion Securities Corporation, Limited.
The first point I want to make is that what we need in this country associated with our railways, if we are going to have this system of nominating a commission and calling them directors, is to see that those men are well paid and that they concentrate their minds upon railway problems. To have these men with all their diverse interests entrusted with this task is a very unwise thing for the country from that point of view. But there is another and, to my mind, a more serious aspect of the situation. As I have read the names of the different companies with which these different gentlemen are associated, I think hon. members will have noticed that there is hardly a requirement of any prime necessity needed by the railways which, if the management wishes, they cannot get from some company in which one of the directors is also a director. I do not know whether this has been done or not; I make no charges against any man without proof of wrong-doing under my hand; but I denounce in unmeasured terms the system such as exists here, because it is quite possible-I aAiuse mo one because I have not the proof-that this forms a little family compact in which the interests of the railway are, perhaps,-I do not know-being sacrificed to the interests of these different companies. It may be perfectly true that Mr. Hanna, when he comes

to consider and to advise the company as to the extension of a line in the Northwest, may remain absolutely uninfluenced by the fact that he is president of the Canadian North Prairie Lands Company. I do not know where those lands are situated; but if we found that a line of the Canadian National railways was being pushed towards those lands, would it not be reasonable for one to be a little suspicious that, in pushing the railway in that way, Mr. Hanna may have, perhaps, unconsciously been affected by the fact that in doing so he would help the Canada North Prairie Lands Company, in which he is a director? As regards locomotives, supposing the National Railways desire locomotives; it may be, for all I know to the contrary, possible that when the Canadian Locomotive company tenders to the National railways for the supply of locomotives, Mr. Hobson knows nothing about the matter at all; that he declines to be present at the meeting of the board where the tenders are opened, and that he does not convey to the Canada Locomotive company any information that he may have as to the price that the Canadian National Railways are willing to pay for the locomotives in question. He himself may be absolutely beyond reproach in this connection; but it is a mistake for the Government of Canada to have, as one of the directors of the Canadian National railways, a gentleman who is also a director of the Canadian Locomotive Company, Limited.
The same principle is in issue when we find that Mr. Robert Hobson is president of the Steel Company of Canada, Limited. If the National Railways should consider it advisable on part of their line to adopt oil-burning locomotives, Mr. Hobson is also a director of the North Star Oil and Refining Company.
Sir Hormisdas Laporte, if the railway supplies its own dining cars, in those parts of the country which are not bone-dry, with light beer to drink, may supply beer of the Frontenac Breweries, Limited, for all I know. I do not know whether he does or not.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: He does.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that he does. I am quite innocent of the information myself. As regards a request for cars, if the railway management want cars, they can, without going outside of the circle of directors, obtain cars from the Eastern Car Company, Limited, of which their director, Col. Thomas Cantley,
102i
is also a director. If they need paint to paint the cars, Brandram-Hennderson, Limited, will no doubt be willing to supply them. If they need coal the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, of which Colonel Thomas Cantley is also a director, will no doubt be prepared to sell to them. As far as Mr. Barnhill's connection with the railway is concerned, I do not know that any companies with which he is connected would be in a position to sell to the Canadian National Railways, because they seem to be mostly publishing companies and land companies. As far as Mr. Wood is concerned, he is a director in such a number of companies that it would appear to be impossible for him to give any real care and attention to the work of the Canadian National Railway system. Now under these conditions is it fair that we should have any limited right of investigation? If Mr. Hobson, Colonel Cantley, and the other gentlemen whose names I have mentioned are high-minded gentlemen, and I have no reason to believe them otherwise, will they not gladly embrace the opportunity to come before this committee and to show that in their administration of the Canadian National Railways they have always considered, first, the interests of the railway, and secondly, the interests of the companies of which they are directors. But I pay that a far better system would be the system which I have urged, without success, I am sorry to say, in this House before, to keep out not only from the Government these interlocking directorates, as I unsuccessfully attempted to do, but also from a department of Government such as this Canadian National Railways' directorate is. I fully appreciated, I trust, as a law student when I sat at the feet of the Minister of Justice, that old French law phrase "Donner et retiner ne vaut," which I might express in homely English as "To give and to withhold at the same time is not worth a continental."
We have had promises of large rights of investigation, but these have been whittled down and whittled down and shaved down by the Prime Minister until, as stated by him, and as commented upon by the Minister of Justice, we find that the committee which the Government are now willing to give is a committee to look into the question of what information should be given by the railways to such a committee, secondly, can such information be given, thirdly, what is the best method of giving this information, what is the best method of

auditing, and for the investigation of what matters should the committee be appointed?
If a committee is to be appointed, and I frankly admit that there are certain advantages in the appointment of a committee, for a committee with the right to call witnesses and for papers could bring before it Mr. Hanna, Mr. E. R. Wood, and Colonel Cantley, in a way in which this House sitting in Committee of the Whole could not do, I say that nothing short of the fullest investigation will satisfy the members of this House who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, and what is of a great deal more importance, will not satisfy the Canadian people whose money is being spent, and who are being heavily taxed. It must be a somewhat galling reflection to men in this country who are paying their income tax to remember that practically the whole, if not the whole, of what we raised for the year 1920 by the income tax will be absorbed by the deficit on the National Railways. We have adopted the system of public ownership, and we must give it a fair chance. Whether we wished to adopt it or not, the system has been adopted, and you cannot give public ownership in this country a fair chance unless the representatives of the people have access to full and complete information about all the operations under public ownership. You cannot give it a fair chance by leaving the control of your railway in the hands of men who have private interests which are not identical with the interests of the railway they are supposed to control and operate, and what we have to do in this House, and what the Liberal party will have to do in this country, is to create a public opnion which will say: We will get the best men that we can for this purpose, and we will see to it that they have no other interests to concern them except the public interest in regard to the railways of this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Nor did I say the committee was going to run the railways.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: You did not say it was going to run the railways, but you did say that in the selection of the committee, if I remember rightly, and I do not want to misinterpret you,-in any event, Hansard will show exactly what was said -provincial lines should be watched. In other words, I understood the hon. gentleman to say: "Don't pick out men in this House who, you may think, can investigate the railways satisfactorily, but see that every province in the Dominion of Canada gets some representation on that committee whether they are fitted for the job or not." That, at any rate, is the interpretation I place on the hon. gentleman's remarks, and it is far from my wish to misrepresent him. The hon. gentleman wants a lot of information brought out. Well, so far as I see, there is no objection to information being given. The Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), has told us that he stands up for the handing out of a large amount of information. But if my memory serves me rightly, in the old days, when my hon. friend sat on the other side of the House, as he is doing now, all matters of this kind were sent to the Public Accounts Committee; but when they got to that committee something happened. There was there what was known as the "blocking brigade"; some three or four self-constituted blockers saw to it that the information sought at that time by our side, who were in opposition, was not forthcoming. I think my hon. friend will recognize the term I have just used, and perhaps he knows some of the men who constituted that committee.

Give their names to the
House.

You had better give the

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE

I was addressing
my remarks more particularly to the hon. member for Halifax who says that he wants all kinds of information.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE

I think it would be well
for you to give the names.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: It is not necessary; the men are well recognized, and they were well known to every one in the House at the time.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: I was not here then and I should be glad to hear the names.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: You did not get into the House in time, but. you had a man representing you here that could speak longer and with more volubility on branch lines than the hon. gentleman himself. I have known him to speak for five hours on the question of branch lines, so what would you do if he attempted to deal with main lines?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Did he not deal with main lines successfully?

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
No, he did not deal with main lines, but branch lines. That gentleman, Mr. Emmerson, used to have a field day every year on branch lines, and certainly he branched out in great shape. Now, my hon. friend from Halifax, who is undertaking to solve this question, apparently thinks that it is possible for this House to constitute a committee that could receive information that could not well be handed to the House. If the committee is not able to do that, I cannot see what particular function it will have. It is perhaps well, as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), has said that every dollar of expenditure should be investigated. I am not sure that that is not a sound business principle, and if it were possible it might be done even with regard to railways. But if that information is to be sought in order to feather arrows to be shot at political archery competitions, I do not think it would be wise. If that information is to be got. in order to help us out of a difficult problem and make non-paying railways a paying enterprise, then by all means it should be granted. But I was considerably nettled to-night to hear the leader of the Opposition calling in such indignant tones for information, information, information!
Let me recall to my hon. friend's mind for a moment what occurred when these

troubles were initiated. By whom were they started? Why are we in this country staggering like weary Titans under this burden? It is because my hon. friend and the hon. gentleman who led him at that time were in a government that launched railway schemes upon the country fifty years in advance of their time. They were told that hundreds of times in the House; they were told that information had not been obtained to warrant this country in building a transcontinental road. What was the reply of the hon. gentleman's leader at that time? "We have mountains of information." Well, what did those mountains of information lead to? They led to the building of what has proved to be the greatest white elephant in the way of railways ever seen in this world. It was known that it would be so, because this railway was projected for purely political purposes, and was never intended as a business proposition, from the time of its inception. It was launched as a political railway for the expenditure of vast sums of money in this country, money which, I say, was wrongfully diverted from the coffers of the country; and if there is any gentleman who should be gentle, and willing to show a little charity and a little confidence in those who are trying to undo this tangle, it is the hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition and who, with his leader in the government of that time, shouldered on to the country vast expenditures not only on the Transcontinental, but on the Canadian Northern. When they put on that $35,000,000 of guarantee on the line traversing the north shore of lake Superior, they placed a heavy burden on the Dominion. And when they undertook to build the Grand Trunk Pacific, it was understood in the first place that it would cost $13,000,000, or at the utmost $60,000,000, and it actually cost $180,000,000. That was the second clamp they put upon the country. Now my hon. friend wants information. Well, I hope he is going to make better use of it than he and his friends did in the years 1903 and 1904, when they got mountains of information and built a railway of 1,800 miles in the wilderness that cannot be made to pay in our time by any board of directors, whether politically appointed or composed of the best business men you can get in this country.
I say we have 1,800 miles of railroad that cannot be made to pay, and it can easily be proved that no body of directors could make that piece of road pay. My hon. friend who leads the Agrarian party (Mr. Crerar) it 
is true, has a receipt all his own for making the national railways pay. I am sorry he is not here to-night to state it, but I have seen it several times in print, and it is worth while recalling to the House just what the hon. gentleman's proposition is. His proposition for making these roads pay is to recapitalize them. They have cost about one thousand million dollars up to date, but they are losing $70,000,000 on operation. Gan any man in the Agrarian party or in any other party in this House, say how these railways are to be made to meet operating expenses by reduction in the capitalization? It cannot be done; and it is childish to suggest it. Whether you capitalize them at one thousand millions, or at one dollar, if they are running at a loss on operating expenses, recapitalization will do absolutely no good, and no one can seriously suggest such a thing. Now, what the country wants to know is what we hs thinking men, are going to do to solve a very difficult and dangerous financial problem, and that is what I want to lend my attention to for a moment. In this respect I am somewhat inclined to agree for once with my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. MeMaster). The hon. gentleman is not often right, and possibly he may be wrong now; but I really feel tempted to agree with him in this respect.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext: Do not do it.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
He says that the
director of a big enterprise controlling some thousand million dollars of the people's money should be prepared to spend all his time, if necessary, in the public interest, in directing the expenditure of that money; and that is but reasonable. The board might be reduced to one-half, and should be comprised of the very best men that could be obtained. I would say that from the general manager down the best men possible should be secured. The general manager should have around him the most efficient staff that money could secure, and they should devote themselves soul and body to the problem of bringing this country out of the darknes and distress in which it is in connection with its railways. To that end, I believe that the policy which my hon. friend has stated with regard to the directorate might very well receive the consideration of the Minister of Railways. I do not want to criticise anything that has been done. It is easy to criticise when a difficult mess of this kind takes place, but I fear myself that the best results have not been obtained from the operation of these

roads. If I were assured of the absolute necessity for it, I would willingly vote another $70,000,000 or more. The Government know the inward operations far better than I do, who sit on the outside and am acquainted with very little that is going on within, but they should consider very carefully indeed whether the Department of Railways and the management of the great railways now known as the Canadian National Railway system, are bringing the best results to the people of Canada which we can reasonably expect. If they are I say support them loyally, endorse heartily everything they do with a view to getting us out of the difficulties we are in. But Mr. Speaker, in order to make these railways pay we have, in my opinion, to have a different spirit not only in this House but amongst the people of the country as well-that is a spirit of loyalty to our own property. By constantly knocking our own property we are not going to build it up. We ought rather to try and boost it, and make helpful suggestions all along the line; we ought to encourage it in the way of traffic, in the way of passengers, and in every possible way that we can. Let us be loyal to our own property and see to it that the best results are obtained from this railway system.
If the committee be appointed, I hope, in order that it may serve a useful purpose, the Prime Minister will make it as wide in its scope as it is possible for it to be, and I believe he will. Because I think it is reasonable-at least as long as deficits occur-to think that the House will want to know what particular expenditures have gone to make up those deficits. I do think that is a proposition that ought to be carefully considered. If the Government were bringing down a seventy million surplus to us each year we might not ask them quite where they got it all; but if they come down with a seventy million odd deficit and ask us to vote the money then I do think that we, as custodians of the public funds should know whether that money is being wisely expended. And if this committee is appointed I think it will act reasonably; it will not unduly harass any department by asking for unnecessary returns, and it will not expect to get information that is going to result in any damage to these roads and that should not be given out. Every one that is a member of a private company knows that there is a very small amount of the expenditure laid before the annual meeting. Even as regards expenditure in lump sums, the company do not tell where
they bought the supplies, or how much they paid for them. That is not the rule. That is the experience in the case of private companies and I am a member of quite a lot of them. I do not know any company which gives that information; and in the case of this great system we ought not to ask for unreasonable information. I do not believe that members if they want to do what is right and want to assist the country out of the deep difficulty in which it is at present, will harass in any way the administration of this great national enterprise. I hope it will be successful, because I think the success of Canada is largely bound up in it. There is nothing at the present time that gives this country more concern than its railway problem and its shipping problem. We are glad to know that our mercantile marine is paying its way and has a surplus even if it is only a small one and we hope the Government railways will soon be in the same position. So far as I am concerned I heartily desire to co-operate in every possible way in making our great national highway the success it ought to be.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac): I wish to say a few words on this all important subject of the Canadian National railways. I was much interested in the remarks which fell from the Minister of Finance when he was discussing the question of parliamentary control. It seems to me that until we solve the problem of getting the members of Parliament and the people of the country educated up to what parliamentary control and public management mean, we are going to be in difficulties as regards our railway problem. There are a great many members of the House who are keenly interested in public ownership and are strongly in favour of it, but apparently have given no thought whatever to the question of public management. I remember very well that in 1918 when this subject was under discussion in the House the Government were quoting whole pages from a certain railway report, of which the Minister of Finance was partly the author to suit their own purpose, and leaving other pages, that did not suit their designs, untouched. In the case of the minister particularly interested in the subject, I was convinced that he had not quite arrived at a sound conclusion as to what might or might not be government control, even after the amount of attention he had given to it. Now, to any man who has given any thought to the subject it goes

without saying that it is impossible to get away from parliamentary control. By the very nature of our governmental institutions it is impossible to ignore, parliamentary control unless you wish to hand the entire supervision of this enterprise over to irresponsible people-that is irresponsible as far as Parliament is concerned-and have no control whatever. You must have one thing or the other; you must have parliamentary control or no control. It is this choice that is confusing the people today. Which are we going to have? Are we to have no control or parliamentary control? Any company of gentlemen who are handling $300,000,000 of the peoples' money should be subject to some control- there should be some control over gentlemen who are handling that much public money. The Estimates provide for $165,000,000, and the railway system earns $125,000,000, making roughly an expenditure of $290,000,000 without allowing for any Supplementary Estimates. The gentlemen who have the control of our railways are, according to the Government, spending this money without restriction to the extent of $300,000,000. The people have come to realize that they have to deal with a serious problem; they have come to realize that first of all the Government and Parliament must take notice of this expenditure. They want to know what is the cause of the deficits. They want to know how these deficits can be eliminated, and the Government raiway system made to earn interest on the investment if possible. The Minister of Finance said this evening that you could not have members of Parliament asking about a station agent some place; but he will not say to me now that it is not legitimate for me to ask the Government why Parliament, through the irresponsible agency referred to, should expend millions of dollars on terminals at Halifax when these expenditures have never been approved by Parliament. The Government came down here and asked for a lump sum to take care of deficits. During the year they were engaged in spending $125,000,000 in any way they pleased, and I am of opinion they are spending a good part of it under the direction of the Minister of Railways. I do not believe that the Board of Management went to Halifax and entered upon an expenditure of several millions of dollars on that undertaking without first consulting the Minister of Railways. I believe that he was advised by the Minister of Railways and Canals.

speechtext: I might answer the hon. member in regard to that. Any expenditure on capital account I gave details of when the Estimates were going through, as to how and where it was to be expended. In so far as operating expenses are concerned, of course, they do not come before us.

maintopic: SUPPLY - CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SPECIAL COMMITTEE OF HOUSE
speechtext:
I am not at all convinced that the minister would mind if I were to refuse to ask any more questions when his Estimates are before the committee, but if he will point out any place in his Estimates in previous years where he mentioned an investment on the Halifax terminals, I believe I would be almost willing to agree not to ask him any more questions on the subject of railways. I would do him that favour. That is one question, the question of contractors who are doubletracking and doing other work in connection with the railways, that comes under capital expenditure; there is no provision made for that in the Estimates except in lump sums such as the minister passed last year at half past two in the morning after delivering a number of speeches all day without giving any information whatever.
Now, the Government may say that it is up to the Opposition to ask for and get information. I think they are justified in saying that, for in my opinion it is the business of the Opposition to get information. But the Government have taken a great proportion of the expenditure of this country entirely out of parliamentary control. The Government come down here with a lump sum for deficits, and they give as little information as possible, and the money voted is spent in any way that the management may see fit, always bearing in mind that it has to co-operate with the Minister of Railways and Canals and his colleagues.
The minister came down and asked the members of this House for suggestions. We are willing to offer suggestions, we are willing to help solve the problem if that is possible; but before attempting to do that the minister will agree with me that the Government must lay their cards on the table, they must be fair to the people and not attempt to do what the Prime Minister has attempted to do to-day. The Prime Min-

ister agreed as a final result of all this discussion, after promising for several days what he was going to do, to appoint a committee. The function of that committee would be to recommend to itself what it should recommend to Parliament, and what Parliament should in turn recommend back to the committee. That in plain language is what the minister said, that this committee would have absolutely no function at all. But if I am not mistaken the Minister of Marine and Fisheries intends to come down to-night to ask the committee to pass Estimates for a department so closely related to the Department of Railways and :Canals that it is not going to give us any information. His department, too, is excluded from furnishing any information pertaining to its expenditure. My hon. friend has been taught some bad lessons by the Minister of Railways and Canals.
The Government should make up their minds as to what they are going to do about this question. It is all very well to ask the Opposition for constructive criticism, but, as I pointed out to the minister last year, we would be very foolish to offer suggestions to a Government that would bungle them. The Prime Minister laughs, but he knows that there never was a Government of this country better able to bungle things. He will not disagree with that surely. This Government has lost more money on railways in the last five years, including this year's deficit, than the total expenditure by all the governments of Canada since Confederation, including the cost of the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental and the Hudson Bay railways. The loss to-day amounts to about $200,000 per day, and my hon. friend's remedy is to appoint a committee to investigate and see what they can do. That is not a solution for the country. The Government must first make up their minds what they are going to do as to furnishing information, about how much they propose to give and how they propose to give it. It is useless to say, "We are going to shift this responsibility on to a committee,"-a committee that will have no responsibility to any person and will merely report. The Government must take responsibility, and if they refuse to give information here, that is for them to answer before the country. But to say that they can appoint a committee to manage our railways, and then to refuse to give the report of that committee to Parliament, is too absurd for the people of Canada to accept. My hon. friend tried to make out that they are
afraid of political control. I will give them a way that will relieve them of a great deal of political control. Bring the whole proposition before the people's representatives, they who vote the money for the enterprise, give it the widest publicity possible, and then you will have no political patronage. If every person is acquainted with what is going on you will have nothing to conceal. Apparently the Government now feel they have something which they must keep back, and the people feel the same way. The Government have given them the lead and the people believe the Government-in this case; in most cases they do not.
The only plan to get away from political patronage is to give the widest possible publicity. Give the Opposition the facts and the information, and you are always protected. If you give the public full information the public may then be able to assist you to obtain better results. If the Government continue muddling along as the Minister of Railways does, the railway deficits in future will be very much greater than they have been. It is too serious a problem for the Government to treat so lightly by appointing a committee that they say will do something. It is for the Government to give information, and the time and place to give it is here and now.
